Project Story

Project kickoff → Problem → What I did → Result

One of the projects I'm most proud of was the Global Direct SAR (Spend Analysis Report) Dashboard for the Finance Leadership team. The goal was to provide a single dashboard to track company spending across regions, departments, and cost categories.

Problem: There were two main challenges — the company followed a fiscal year from August to July, so normal YTD calculations would not work, and data came from multiple countries and currencies, requiring consistent currency conversion.

What I did: I implemented currency conversion logic in SQL views using exchange rates provided by the finance team. In Power BI, I created a Fiscal Calendar and developed DAX measures for Fiscal YTD, Budget YTD, and Prior Year Comparison. I also implemented Dynamic RLS using USERPRINCIPALNAME() so users could only see data relevant to their role.

Result: The finance team moved away from manual Excel reconciliation and started using a trusted dashboard for financial reporting and decision-making.

Biggest Challenge — Revenue Dashboard Issue

One of the biggest challenges I faced was in an existing Revenue Dashboard. The summary revenue numbers were correct, but when users drilled down to Product Group level, the numbers did not match the source system. The finance team was using these numbers for margin analysis and business decisions, so accuracy was critical.

I analyzed the data model, relationships, and DAX measures, and found that some relationships were incorrect and a few DAX measures were not handling filter context properly. I redesigned the model using Star Schema principles, fixed the relationships, and updated the DAX measures. I validated the results with finance users and compared the dashboard numbers against source data until everything matched.

The business regained confidence in the dashboard and no longer needed manual Excel validation, improving reporting efficiency.

FABRIC IN PASSAGE

Microsoft Fabric is Microsoft's unified end-to-end analytics platform that brings together Data Factory, Data Engineering, Data Warehouse, Data Science, Real-Time Analytics, and Power BI into a single SaaS solution. Before Fabric, organizations typically used multiple separate services such as Azure Data Factory for ETL, Azure Synapse for warehousing and analytics, Azure Data Lake for storage, and Power BI for reporting. Managing multiple tools increased complexity, integration effort, security management, and cost.

Fabric solves this by providing a single platform with OneLake as the centralized storage layer. OneLake acts like OneDrive for enterprise data, allowing all Fabric workloads to access the same data without creating multiple copies.

One of the key concepts in Fabric is the Lakehouse, which combines the flexibility of a Data Lake with the performance of a Data Warehouse. It can store structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data while supporting both SQL and Spark workloads.

For reporting, Fabric introduces Direct Lake mode, where Power BI reads data directly from OneLake. This provides near Import-mode performance without needing to duplicate data or rely on slower DirectQuery queries.

Fabric also supports Dataflow Gen2 and Data Factory pipelines for ETL processes, Warehouses for SQL analytics, and Real-Time Analytics for streaming and log data. Since everything is integrated into one platform, organizations get better governance, simplified architecture, reduced maintenance, improved performance, and faster development cycles.

Although my primary hands-on experience is with Power BI, I understand how Fabric unifies the modern data platform and enables scalable analytics through OneLake, Lakehouse, Warehouses, and Direct Lake integration.

TOP FABRIC QUESTIONS ASKED

1. What is Microsoft Fabric?

Microsoft Fabric is an end-to-end unified analytics platform that combines Data Engineering, Data Factory, Data Science, Data Warehouse, Real-Time Analytics, and Power BI into a single SaaS solution built on OneLake.

2. Why did Microsoft introduce Fabric?

Microsoft introduced Fabric to eliminate data silos and reduce the need for multiple tools. It provides a single platform for data integration, storage, analytics, and reporting with centralized governance.

3. What are the major workloads in Microsoft Fabric?

The major workloads are Data Factory, Data Engineering, Data Science, Data Warehouse, Real-Time Analytics, Power BI, and Industry Solutions. All workloads use the same OneLake storage layer.

4. What is OneLake?

OneLake is Fabric's unified data lake that acts as a single source of truth for all organizational data. It eliminates data duplication and allows all Fabric workloads to access the same data.

5. What is a Lakehouse?

A Lakehouse combines the scalability of a Data Lake with the management and querying capabilities of a Data Warehouse. It can store structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data.

6. Difference Between Lakehouse and Data Warehouse?

A Lakehouse supports all data types and is optimized for analytics and data engineering, whereas a Data Warehouse primarily stores structured data and is optimized for BI reporting and SQL queries.

7. What is Direct Lake Mode?

Direct Lake allows Power BI to query data directly from OneLake without importing data into Power BI memory, providing near Import-mode performance with real-time access.

8. Difference Between Import, DirectQuery, and Direct Lake?

Import loads data into Power BI memory for best performance. DirectQuery queries the source system in real time but can be slower. Direct Lake reads directly from OneLake, offering near-import performance without data duplication.

9. What is Delta Lake?

Delta Lake is an open-source storage format that adds ACID transactions, versioning, and data reliability to data lakes. Fabric stores Lakehouse tables in Delta format.

10. What is a Fabric Capacity?

Fabric Capacity is dedicated compute power that runs Fabric workloads. It determines performance, concurrency, and resource availability and is available through F-SKUs such as F2, F64, and F128.

11. What is Data Factory in Fabric?

Data Factory is Fabric's data integration service used to ingest, transform, and orchestrate data from multiple sources using pipelines and Dataflow Gen2.

12. What is a Pipeline in Fabric?

A Pipeline is a workflow orchestration tool used to automate data movement and transformation activities, similar to Azure Data Factory pipelines.

13. What is a Dataflow Gen2?

Dataflow Gen2 is a low-code ETL tool that uses Power Query for data transformation and stores processed data directly in OneLake for further analytics.

14. How is Fabric different from Synapse?

Fabric is a fully integrated SaaS platform with OneLake and Power BI built in, whereas Synapse requires separate services and more manual integration between components.

15. What is Mirroring in Fabric?

Mirroring continuously replicates data from external databases such as Azure SQL Database into OneLake with minimal latency, enabling near real-time analytics.

16. What is Real-Time Analytics?

Real-Time Analytics is used to analyze streaming and event-based data with low latency, making it suitable for IoT, logs, monitoring, and operational analytics.

17. What is KQL Database?

A KQL Database is an analytics database that uses Kusto Query Language (KQL) for fast querying of large volumes of telemetry, log, and time-series data.

18. How does Power BI integrate with Fabric?

Power BI is natively integrated into Fabric and can directly connect to Lakehouse, Warehouse, and OneLake data using Import, DirectQuery, or Direct Lake modes.

19. What are the benefits of Fabric?

Key benefits include a unified platform, OneLake storage, reduced data duplication, simplified governance, real-time analytics, seamless Power BI integration, and lower operational complexity.

20. What Fabric features have you used?

I have worked with Lakehouse, Dataflow Gen2, Pipelines, OneLake, Direct Lake mode, and Power BI integration. I used them for data ingestion, transformation, storage, and building reporting solutions with near real-time analytics.

I usually start by understanding the business objective and the problem stakeholders are trying to solve, rather than directly starting with the report. I discuss the required KPIs, filters, business rules, data sources, expected output, and target users, and document the requirements clearly. If the requirement is ambiguous, I ask focused questions, confirm the business logic with the stakeholder, and create a clear understanding of what should be delivered.

Once the requirements are clear, I translate them into SQL logic, data-model requirements, DAX measures, KPIs, and Power BI visuals. For example, for inventory reporting, I would clarify metrics such as WOC, In-Stock %, and Stockout Rate and then build the report around those business definitions. I also work iteratively with stakeholders — sharing the initial report, collecting feedback, and incorporating approved change requests.

For validation and UAT, I first validate the data and KPI calculations against SQL/source data, then share the report with business users in the UAT environment. I support stakeholders during UAT, resolve any data, calculation, or visualization issues, and make sure the final numbers match the agreed business definitions before production deployment. The project documentation also describes UAT as involving sample-data testing, DAX unit testing, business-user sign-off on KPIs, and validation before production deployment.

I lead with the business impact, not the mechanism — “this DC is stocking out 30% more often than it should” before “because of an incorrect allocation weighting.” I use visuals and concrete comparisons rather than jargon, and I check understanding by asking them to restate the takeaway back to me before I move on.

I combine a short live walkthrough of the dashboard with a one-page quick-reference guide covering what each visual means and how to filter it, plus a recorded video for anyone who misses the session. I also hold informal office hours in the first couple of weeks after launch, since most real questions surface only once people start using it on live data.

During the initial adoption period I also actively collect feedback on usability, missing requirements, confusing KPIs, and performance issues — separating actual defects from enhancement requests and prioritizing the approved changes.

I triage by business impact first — is this a wrong number stakeholders are actively using, or a cosmetic issue? For anything affecting decisions, I communicate the issue and expected fix timeline immediately rather than silently patching it, do root cause analysis rather than a surface fix, and add a validation check afterward so the same class of bug doesn’t recur.

That I take ownership beyond what’s assigned — I built the vw_kpi_master view and the DC allocation fix proactively because I saw the underlying data problem, not because someone asked for a specific dashboard. For the SAR project, I worked off a Business Requirements Document that captured the business objectives, reporting requirements, KPIs, and stakeholder expectations — things like the fiscal calendar logic (August–July year), which currencies needed conversion, and the RLS access rules per region. Alongside that, I also maintain a mapping document — mapping each report field/KPI back to its source table and the business logic or SQL view that produces it, so there's a single source of truth connecting "what the business asked for" to "where it comes from in the data." This is especially useful during UAT, since if a stakeholder questions a number, I can trace it straight back to the source logic instead of re-deriving it from scratch, and it also makes handover or future maintenance much easier for anyone else picking up the report.

What is it? Trend Analysis identifies whether a KPI is increasing, decreasing, or remaining stable over time. It helps understand long-term business performance.

Where used? Sales, Revenue, Inventory, Demand Forecasting.

Real Case: Monthly sales increased from ₹10M to ₹15M over six months.

Jan = ₹10M
Feb = ₹11M
Mar = ₹12M
Apr = ₹13M

Conclusion: Upward Sales Trend.

Where used? Sales decline, Stockouts, KPI drops, Production Issues.

Formula: Variance = Actual − Target

What is it? Identifying recurring behaviors, relationships, or trends in data. Helps uncover business insights.

Where used? Sales Analysis, Customer Behavior, Inventory Planning.

Real Case: Stockouts increase every weekend — a recurring pattern identified.

Saturday → High Demand
Sunday → High Demand
Monday → Normal

Pattern = Weekend Demand Spike.

Where used? Revenue, Margin, Inventory, Forecast Accuracy.

What is it? Measures how much each category, product, region, or customer contributes to a KPI.

Where used? Revenue Analysis, Profit Analysis, Business Reviews.

Real Case: North Region = 40% Revenue, South Region = 25% Revenue — North contributes the most.

Formula: Contribution % = Region Sales ÷ Total Sales

What is it? States that roughly 80% of outcomes come from 20% of causes.

Where used? Sales, Inventory, Customer Analysis.

Real Case: 20% of products generate 80% of revenue.

Top 100 Products → ₹8M Revenue

Interview Insight: Focus business efforts on the critical 20%.

What is it? Measures how close forecasted values are to actual values. Evaluates forecasting effectiveness.

Where used? Demand Planning, Supply Chain, Inventory Management.

Real Case: Forecast = 1000 Units, Actual = 950 Units — forecast performed well.

Formula: Forecast Accuracy = 1 − ABS(Forecast − Actual) ÷ Actual

"Sales dropped 15% because 3 top-selling products were out of stock in the South Region. Replenishing inventory could recover approximately ₹500K revenue."

In my Power BI projects, I have mainly worked with SQL Server/SSMS, JDA allocation data, ODBMS, store inventory, and sales/POS data. In the retail project, these sources provided information such as product, sales, inventory, purchase orders, and distribution-center allocation data. The production data was stored in SQL tables, while CSV files were mainly used as snapshots for analysis and validation.

Yes, I have worked with multiple data sources. My approach was to bring the required data into the SQL/reporting layer, perform data cleaning, validation, joins, and business transformations using SQL, and then connect Power BI to the prepared reporting views. Power Query was mainly used for final transformations such as column selection and data types, while maintaining query folding wherever possible.

For connectivity, the main dashboards used Import Mode because performance was important and the data was refreshed on a schedule. For scenarios requiring current data, DirectQuery was used for real-time DC stock monitoring. The Power BI Gateway connected the on-premise SQL Server to Power BI Service for scheduled refreshes.

Multiple sources → SQL/ETL → validation & transformation → Power BI/Power Query → data model → DAX → dashboard → Power BI Service

Power Apps

"Power Apps is a low-code Microsoft platform used to build custom business applications. In my project, I would use it when users need to enter or update operational data instead of directly modifying the database. For example, in a retail project, store users can use a Power App to report stock issues, update inventory adjustments, or raise replenishment requests. The app can connect to sources like SharePoint, Dataverse, SQL Server, or Power BI, so it becomes an interactive front end for the business process."

Real-life case: "For example, if a store identifies a stock discrepancy, they can open a Power App, select the SKU and store, enter the actual quantity, and submit it. That information can then be stored and used in Power BI reporting."

Power Automate

"Power Automate is used to automate repetitive business processes and notifications across Microsoft and other systems. For example, in a retail environment, if inventory for a product falls below the defined threshold, Power Automate can trigger an alert to the inventory team through Teams or email. It can also automate approvals, data movement, scheduled refresh-related processes, and notifications. The main benefit is reducing manual work and making the process faster and more reliable."

Real-life case: "For example, when a store submits a stock adjustment through Power Apps, Power Automate can automatically send it to the manager for approval and notify the inventory team after approval."

ETL stands for Extract, Transform, and Load. In my projects, data is extracted from sources like SQL Server and Excel files, transformed using Power Query by cleaning data, handling nulls, removing duplicates, and applying business rules, and then loaded into the Power BI data model for reporting. ETL ensures data quality, consistency, and accuracy before it is used for analysis and dashboarding. It is a critical step for creating reliable business reports.

ETL stands for Extract, Transform, and Load, where data is cleaned and transformed before loading into the target system. ELT stands for Extract, Load, and Transform, where raw data is first loaded into a data warehouse or lake and then transformed using its compute power. Traditional data warehouses commonly use ETL, while modern cloud platforms like Microsoft Fabric, Snowflake, and Databricks mostly use ELT because it scales better for large datasets.

Real Project Example

ETL:

SQL Server → Power Query transformations → Power BI Model

ELT:

SQL Server → Data Lake/Warehouse → Transform using SQL/Fabric/Dataflows → Reporting

In my project, I treated data quality and validation as an important step before the data reached the Power BI dashboard. I first validated the source data using SQL by checking for NULL values, duplicate records, incorrect formats, unexpected values, and record-count inconsistencies. For duplicate or missing records, I identified the affected records using SQL and either removed duplicates or handled NULLs according to the business rule before using the data for reporting. The project documentation specifically includes duplicate-PO and JDA data-quality checks as part of the SQL validation process.

For KPI validation, I independently calculated the KPI using SQL and then compared the result with the corresponding Power BI/DAX measure. For example, for WOC, In-Stock %, and other inventory KPIs, I checked the Power BI results against the underlying SQL data and business definitions. If there was a mismatch, I traced it through the SQL logic, relationships, filter context, and DAX calculation.

For dashboard accuracy, I performed source-to-report validation by checking record counts, totals, filters, KPI values, and different business scenarios. I also validated that slicers and report filters produced the expected results.

For UAT, after internal testing and DAX validation, I moved the report to the UAT environment and worked with business users to validate the KPIs and report functionality. Stakeholders reviewed the numbers against their business expectations, provided feedback, and I resolved any issues before getting their sign-off. The documented process includes sample-data testing, DAX unit testing, UAT with business-user KPI sign-off, and then production deployment.

Before production, my final process was:

Source validation → SQL data-quality checks → Duplicate/NULL checks → KPI validation → Power BI/DAX validation → Report testing → UAT → Stakeholder sign-off → Production deployment → Post-deployment refresh validation

I also used refresh monitoring in production. For example, when a Gateway refresh failed and the dashboard continued showing old allocation numbers, I added a Last Refreshed indicator and a data-validation check to detect silent refresh failures.

In my project, I designed a Star Schema, which is the main data model I used for the Power BI reporting solution. The model had central fact tables containing measurable business data, such as Sales and Inventory, surrounded by dimension tables such as Products, Stores, and Date. For example, the Sales fact contained fields such as product_id, store_id, date_id, units_sold, and net_revenue, while the Product dimension contained attributes such as category, season, section, price, material, and origin.

I have primarily worked with Star Schema, and the project documentation also covers concepts such as Snowflake Schema and Slowly Changing Dimensions. I prefer Star Schema in Power BI because relationships are simpler, filter propagation is cleaner, and DAX calculations are easier to maintain.

When designing the model, I first identified the business grain of each fact table, then separated measurable transactional data from descriptive attributes. I created relationships between the dimensions and fact tables using keys, generally with one-to-many relationships, and added a proper Date table for time-based analysis. I then built DAX measures such as WOC, In-Stock %, MOM Revenue, YTD Sales, and Store Sales Rank on top of the model.

I also focused on performance while designing the model by removing unnecessary columns, using appropriate data types, keeping relationships simple, and avoiding unnecessary bidirectional filtering. This helped create a model that was easier to maintain and performed well for the business dashboards.

Define business grain → Identify facts & dimensions → Build Star Schema → Create relationships → Add Date table → Validate data → Create DAX measures → Optimize the model → Build reports

I used SQL and Power BI together as part of the complete reporting workflow on the Global Direct SAR (Spend Analysis Report) Dashboard. I primarily used SQL for data extraction, cleaning, validation, joins, aggregations, KPI calculations, and preparing the data before it was consumed by Power BI. I worked with tables such as Expense Transactions, Budget Data, Prior Year Historical Data, and Currency Exchange Rates, and used SQL to analyze spend, budget variance, currency-standardized revenue, and other finance KPIs across regions and departments.

I created SQL views to standardize and prepare the business logic before connecting Power BI. For example, I built views to combine and transform data into reporting-ready datasets, including a vw_currency_conversion view that standardized multi-region spend into a single reporting currency, and a vw_revenue_standard view that aligned Finance and Operations revenue definitions so both teams could use a consistent source of truth.

I preferred using Views instead of writing the complete SQL logic directly in Power BI because the business logic could be centralized, reused across reports, easier to validate, and maintained at the SQL/reporting layer. It also allowed Power BI to consume a cleaner, reporting-ready dataset instead of repeatedly processing complex joins and transformations.

For SQL performance, I focused on filtering and aggregating data at the SQL layer, using appropriate joins, avoiding unnecessary columns, and preparing aggregated/reporting views before Power BI consumed the data. This reduced the amount of raw data Power BI had to process and improved overall report performance. I generally pushed aggregations into SQL rather than making Power BI process large raw tables.

SQL → Extract & Clean → Join & Validate → Create Reporting Views → Power BI Data Model → DAX → Dashboard

Business Impact: Centralizing currency conversion and business logic in SQL views gave finance leadership a single, trusted source of truth for spend reporting, and kept Power BI refresh times and DAX complexity low even as more regions and reports were added.

I have hands-on experience developing Power BI dashboards for a Corporate Finance and FP&A client, mainly covering company-wide spend, budget vs. actuals, prior year comparison, and cost-center/region performance on the Global Direct SAR (Spend Analysis Report) Dashboard. I worked primarily with MS SQL Server data, where finance data from multiple regional financial systems was consolidated into fact and dimension tables, and I used SQL Views and Power Query to prepare the reporting layer, including currency conversion logic. I followed a Star Schema approach and developed DAX measures for KPIs such as Fiscal YTD Actuals, Budget YTD, Prior Year Comparison, Variance %, and Expense as % of Sales. For the project architecture, the flow was Regional Financial Systems → SQL Server → SQL Views (Currency Conversion & Business Logic) → Power BI Power Query → Semantic Model → DAX → Reports/Dashboards. One challenging area was ensuring currency-converted spend and budget variance KPIs were accurate across different regions and fiscal periods, so I validated the SQL results against Power BI measures and corrected model relationships and calculation logic where required. For deployment, I understand the Dev → Test/UAT → Production approach, where reports are validated in development, finance business users perform UAT, and the approved version is published to Production with appropriate refresh and Dynamic RLS configuration. My core focus has been building reliable dashboards, validating business logic, optimizing performance and supporting production reporting.

In my project, I developed Power BI dashboards for inventory, allocation, sales, and supply-chain monitoring. The main purpose was to give Buying, Planning, Merchandising, Supply Chain, and Distribution teams a single view of inventory health and help them identify stockout, overstock, and allocation issues. I worked with KPIs such as WOC, In-Stock %, Stockout Rate, Sell-Through %, Allocation Accuracy, Forecast Accuracy, DC Utilization, Inventory Value, Revenue, and Gross Margin %.

For example, WOC (Weeks of Cover) measures how many weeks the available inventory is expected to last. I calculated it using SOH + SOO divided by average weekly sales, based on the last eight weeks of sales. Stockout Rate measures the percentage of SKUs with no available stock, while Sell-Through Rate measures the percentage of purchased/bought units that were actually sold. Allocation Accuracy measures how closely the actual allocation matches the optimal allocation, and Forecast Accuracy measures how closely actual demand matches the forecast. DC Utilization indicates how effectively distribution-center capacity or stock is being utilized. Inventory Value represents the monetary value of inventory, and Gross Margin % measures profitability after COGS. The project documentation specifically defines WOC, In-Stock %, Stockout, Sell-Through, GMROI, and Inventory Turn with their formulas and business interpretation.

I implemented the KPI calculations mainly through SQL and DAX measures. For example, the DAX WOC measure calculates total stock as SOH plus SOO and divides it by average weekly sales, while In-Stock % is calculated using SKUs where SOH is greater than zero.

To ensure accuracy, I first validated the source data and SQL calculations, then compared the Power BI KPI results against SQL outputs and business expectations. During UAT, I worked with stakeholders to validate the KPI definitions and report numbers before production deployment. I also used data-quality checks and refresh validation to identify issues.

For visualization, I selected the visual based on the business question. KPI cards were used for critical metrics such as WOC and Stockout Rate, line charts for trends, bar/column charts for category and seasonal comparisons, matrices for detailed product analysis, and gauges for DC utilization. I also used conditional formatting for WOC status and bookmarks to switch between stockout and excess-inventory views.

The overall business value was that the dashboards converted complex inventory and allocation data into actionable insights. Instead of manually checking multiple sources, business teams could quickly identify where stock was too low, where inventory was excessive, and where allocation needed attention. This supported faster replenishment, better allocation decisions, and improved inventory visibility. My resume reflects the resulting impact as a 30% reduction in stockouts, 10% improvement in allocation accuracy, and 15% increase in revenue.

Dashboard → KPIs → SQL/DAX calculation → Validation → Right visualization → Business action → Measurable impact

In my Cognizant retail supply-chain project, I developed Power BI dashboards focused on sales, inventory, allocation, replenishment, and store/DC performance. The data originated from ERP systems and was loaded into SQL Server through SSIS pipelines by the data engineering team. I used SQL Views and Power Query for data preparation, built a Star Schema data model with fact and dimension tables, and created DAX measures for KPIs such as Revenue, Inventory Value, In-Stock %, Stockout Rate, Sell-Through %, Allocation Accuracy, and Weeks of Cover (WOC).

For visualization, I used KPI Cards to display executive-level metrics, Line Charts to analyze sales and inventory trends over time, Clustered Bar Charts to compare store, region, and DC performance, Matrix visuals for detailed product-store inventory analysis, Donut Charts for category contribution, Slicers for self-service filtering, and Conditional Formatting to highlight inventory risks such as stockouts and low WOC. I also implemented drill-through functionality so users could navigate from summary-level KPIs to detailed store and product analysis.

One of the key challenges was ensuring KPI consistency and dashboard performance. I standardized business logic in SQL Views, validated Power BI calculations against SQL outputs, optimized DAX measures, and followed Star Schema modeling best practices. The dashboards helped business users monitor inventory health, allocation effectiveness, stockouts, and replenishment decisions, enabling data-driven supply-chain planning and operational decision-making.

ERP data → SSIS load to SQL Server → SQL Views & Power Query → Star Schema model → DAX KPIs → Power BI visuals (Cards, Line, Bar, Matrix, Donut, Drill-through) → business decision-making

In my project, I used Power Query mainly for data preparation and transformation, while I used DAX for analytical calculations and dynamic KPIs. Power Query handled tasks such as selecting required columns, setting data types, and performing final transformations before loading the data into the Power BI model. I also tried to maintain query folding by keeping major transformations in SQL views and using Power Query mainly for the final preparation steps.

For DAX, I created measures such as MOM Revenue Growth, YTD Sales, In-Stock %, WOC, and Store Sales Rank. For example, my WOC measure calculated total stock as SOH + SOO and divided it by average weekly sales based on the last eight weeks.

One of the more challenging DAX problems I faced was a regional sales-percentage measure that was giving the correct overall total but incorrect regional values. I traced the issue to the use of ALL(), which was removing the region filter. I corrected the measure by removing only the required product-level filter so that the region filter was preserved.

The main DAX functions I used were CALCULATE(), SUM(), DIVIDE(), FILTER(), DATEADD(), DATESYTD(), DATESINPERIOD(), RANKX(), ALL(), ALLEXCEPT(), and VAR. I used them for time intelligence, KPI calculations, ranking, filter manipulation, and percentage calculations.

For DAX optimization, I used variables with VAR to avoid repeated calculations, preferred efficient filter-context logic with CALCULATE(), avoided unnecessary iterators such as SUMX() over large fact tables, and pushed heavy aggregation work into SQL where possible. I also used measures instead of unnecessary calculated columns because measures are evaluated dynamically based on filter context.

Power Query = Prepare & Transform Data → Data Model → DAX = Calculate & Analyze → KPIs → Dashboard

When I face a slow Power BI report, I first identify the bottleneck rather than changing everything at once. I use Performance Analyzer to identify slow visuals and DAX queries, then check the data model, SQL queries, relationships, and refresh process.

In my project, I optimized performance at multiple levels. At the SQL level, I pushed aggregations and transformations into SQL views so that Power BI did not have to process unnecessary raw data. At the data-model level, I removed unused columns, used appropriate data types, maintained a clean star schema, and avoided unnecessary bidirectional relationships. At the DAX level, I used measures appropriately, optimized CALCULATE() logic, used VAR to avoid repeated calculations, and avoided unnecessary iteration over large fact tables. The project documentation specifically recommends these approaches for large Power BI models.

For refresh performance, I used Incremental Refresh, so instead of refreshing the complete historical dataset every time, only the required recent data was refreshed. In the documented project example, this reduced the refresh time from around 40 minutes to approximately 4 minutes.

I also monitored the refresh and Gateway process because a report can appear incorrect or slow when the underlying dataset has not refreshed properly. In one production issue, the Gateway refresh failed silently, so I added a Last Refreshed indicator and a validation check comparing current and previous allocation records.

Identify bottleneck → Optimize SQL → Optimize data model → Optimize DAX → Optimize visuals → Enable Incremental Refresh → Monitor Gateway/refresh → Validate performance

The key principle I follow is "optimize the data before optimizing the visuals."

In my project, after development and internal validation, I published the Power BI report to the appropriate Power BI Service workspace and followed the Dev → Test/UAT → Production deployment process. The dataset was deployed first, followed by the report, and production refresh schedules and security settings were configured before the final release.

For data refresh, the main dashboards used Import Mode, so the data was refreshed on a scheduled basis. An Enterprise Power BI Gateway connected the on-premise SQL Server to Power BI Service, with the documented project setup using a 6 AM nightly refresh before the morning business reviews.

For sharing, I published the reports to Power BI Service so that the relevant Buying, Planning, Supply Chain, Finance, DC Operations, and leadership teams could access the reports.

For access management, I used workspace permissions and Row-Level Security (RLS) where required. In the inventory dashboard, I implemented Dynamic RLS using a UserRegion table and USERPRINCIPALNAME(), so users automatically saw data for their assigned region. I tested the roles using View as Role before publishing.

Develop → Test/UAT → Publish → Configure Gateway & Refresh → Apply Security/RLS → Share with Users → Monitor Production

In my project, I used Power BI Service for publishing, sharing, security, and refresh management. For security, I implemented Dynamic Row-Level Security (RLS). I created a UserRegion mapping table containing user email and region, and used USERPRINCIPALNAME() with LOOKUPVALUE() so that each user automatically saw only the data for their assigned region. I tested the role using View as Role in Power BI Desktop before publishing.

For RLS vs OLS, RLS controls which rows of data a user can see, whereas OLS is used to restrict access to specific tables or columns. My documented project experience specifically covers Dynamic RLS; OLS is not documented as an implemented project feature, so I would present OLS as a Power BI security concept rather than claim that I implemented it.

A Power BI workspace is the collaborative environment where reports, semantic models, dashboards, and other Power BI content are developed and managed. A Power BI App is a packaged, controlled way of distributing selected content from a workspace to business users.

A report is a multi-page interactive Power BI document containing visuals, filters, drill-through, and other interactions, while a dashboard is a single-page canvas in Power BI Service made up of pinned tiles. In my project, I developed multi-page reports and provided executives with KPI dashboard views.

For navigation, drill-down allows users to move to a more detailed level within the same visual — for example, Year → Quarter → Month → Day. Drill-through takes the user to a separate detail page while carrying the selected filter context. I used drill-down for time-based analysis and drill-through for detailed DC or stockout investigation.

I used bookmarks when I wanted to provide different report views without creating separate pages. For example, my dashboard used a bookmark to toggle between stockout and excess-inventory views with a button.

For data refresh, the main reports used Import Mode with scheduled refresh through the Enterprise Power BI Gateway, which connected the on-premise SQL Server to Power BI Service. The documented project setup used a nightly refresh at 6 AM. I also monitored refresh status and added a Last Refreshed indicator and validation check to identify failed or stale refreshes.

RLS → control rows | OLS → control objects/columns | Workspace → manage content | App → distribute content | Report → multi-page analysis | Dashboard → single-page KPI view | Drill-down → same visual | Drill-through → detail page | Bookmarks → alternate views | Gateway → scheduled refresh

During the project, several documents were maintained throughout the project lifecycle.

  • Business Requirement Document (BRD) — Captured business objectives, reporting requirements, KPIs, and stakeholder expectations.
  • Functional Requirement Document (FRD) — Detailed report functionality, calculations, filters, drill-down requirements, and business rules.
  • Source-to-Target Mapping (STM) — Mapped source system fields to Power BI data model fields and transformations.
  • Data Dictionary — Documented table names, column definitions, data types, and business meanings.
  • Technical Design Document (TDD) — Included architecture, data flow, SQL views, data model design, DAX logic, and security implementation.
  • Test Cases / UAT Document — Used for validating dashboard calculations and obtaining business sign-off.
  • RLS Security Matrix — Defined user roles, access levels, and Row-Level Security rules.
  • Deployment & Release Document — Contained deployment steps, refresh schedules, gateway configuration, and production release details.
  • User Guide / Knowledge Transfer Document — Explained dashboard navigation, filters, KPIs, and report usage for end users.

I understand the broader Microsoft analytics ecosystem around Power BI. Data can be moved using Azure Data Factory into ADLS Gen2 or OneLake, transformed in Azure Synapse or Microsoft Fabric, and visualized in Power BI. Power Apps can be embedded into reports for user actions, Dataverse can store business data, and Power Automate can automate approvals and notifications. For on-premises data sources, Power BI uses an On-Premises Data Gateway for secure refreshes. This provides an end-to-end analytics solution across Azure and the Microsoft Power Platform.

What is Microsoft Azure? Microsoft Azure is a cloud computing platform provided by Microsoft that offers services for computing, storage, networking, databases, analytics, AI, and application hosting. It allows organizations to build, deploy, and manage applications without maintaining physical infrastructure.

Why is Azure Used?

  • Host applications and websites
  • Store and process large amounts of data
  • Build data warehouses and analytics solutions
  • Run ETL/ELT pipelines
  • Implement AI/ML solutions
  • Disaster recovery and backup

Interview One-Liner

"Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform that provides computing, storage, networking, database, analytics, and AI services. In data projects, I've used Azure services such as Data Factory, Data Lake, Synapse, and Power BI to build scalable data pipelines and reporting solutions."

1. SQL — Allocation & Inventory Analysis

One of the major challenges I faced was that some stores were experiencing stockouts even though inventory was available across the network. My responsibility was to identify whether the root cause was demand, supply or allocation. I used SQL joins, aggregations and business logic across inventory, allocation, store and DC data and compared the inventory allocated to each DC against the stores they were serving. For example, I identified that one DC was receiving around 70% of the inventory while serving around 50% of the stores, indicating an allocation imbalance. My analysis supported the 60/30/10 rebalancing recommendation, which was associated with approximately 30% reduction in stockouts and 10% improvement in allocation accuracy.

2. Power BI — KPI, DAX & Data Modeling

One of the Power BI challenges was maintaining accurate and consistent KPI calculations across different business views. I was responsible for building a reliable model and ensuring KPIs such as WOC, Stockout Rate, In-Stock %, Sell-Through and Allocation Accuracy were calculated correctly. I followed a Star Schema, created the required relationships and developed reusable DAX measures, and then validated the Power BI results against SQL outputs. For example, I used WOC to identify stores with low inventory coverage and potential stockout risk versus stores with excess inventory, helping planners make better allocation and replenishment decisions. This resulted in a more reliable and consistent reporting layer for the business.

3. SQL + Power BI — Performance Optimization

Another challenge was maintaining good dashboard performance while working with retail sales, inventory and allocation data. I optimized the SQL Views, data model and DAX calculations, reduced unnecessary data and primarily used Import Mode for the core dashboards because they had nightly refresh requirements. For example, instead of performing every KPI calculation inside Power BI, I standardized reusable reporting logic in SQL Views such as vw_kpi_master and then consumed the prepared data in Power BI. For the specific requirement of real-time DC stock monitoring, I used DirectQuery. This helped create a performance-focused reporting architecture while still meeting the business requirements.

4. Inter-Store Transfer — Inventory Rebalancing

Another challenge was that some stores had excess inventory while other stores had shortages of the same product. I was responsible for identifying potential Inter-Store Transfer opportunities before recommending additional procurement. I used SQL to compare product-level inventory across stores and applied conditions such as SOH greater than 100 for excess stores and below 20 for needy stores, while keeping a safety-stock buffer at the source store. For example, if Store A had excess units of a product while Store B had very low stock, the analysis could identify Store A → Store B as a potential transfer. This created a structured approach to inventory rebalancing and stockout prevention.

5. KPI/Data Validation — SQL vs Power BI

One challenge was ensuring that the numbers shown in Power BI were consistent with the underlying SQL data. When a KPI or total did not match, I traced the data flow from the SQL base tables and Views through Power Query, the Power BI model and DAX measures. For example, for an inventory KPI, I would compare the SQL-level aggregation with the Power BI result and check for duplicate records, incorrect relationships, filters or transformation issues. I then corrected the relevant logic and revalidated the result. This helped ensure that the dashboards provided accurate and trusted numbers to business users.

We also conducted retrospectives to identify process improvements. My responsibilities included SQL development, Power BI reporting, dashboard enhancements, defect fixes, UAT support, and production support.

I have hands-on exposure to SSIS as part of the ETL layer feeding my SQL/Power BI reporting solutions. Below are the key SSIS concepts and questions I keep ready for interviews.

SSIS, or SQL Server Integration Services, is Microsoft's ETL tool used to extract data from multiple sources, transform and cleanse it based on business rules, and load it into target systems like data warehouses. It is commonly used for data migration, data integration, and automating scheduled data loads for reporting and analytics.

Control Flow manages the workflow of an SSIS package, such as executing SQL queries, sending emails, or running tasks in sequence. Data Flow is where the actual ETL happens—it extracts data from sources, applies transformations like Lookup or Derived Column, and loads it into destinations.

Incremental Load means loading only new or changed records instead of reloading the entire dataset. Typically, we use a Last Modified Date or watermark column to identify changes. This significantly reduces load time and improves performance for large datasets.

Lookup Transformation is used to match data from a source with a reference table. For example, matching Product IDs from a sales file with a Product Dimension table to retrieve Product Names or Category information. It's one of the most commonly used transformations in SSIS.

I typically use Error Output to redirect failed records into an error table for analysis, while valid records continue processing. I also implement logging and Event Handlers such as OnError to capture detailed failure information and support troubleshooting.

To improve performance, I use incremental loads, filter data at the source, remove unnecessary columns, optimize lookups using caching, enable Fast Load for destinations, and avoid expensive transformations like Sort whenever possible.

Variables are used within the package during execution to store dynamic values such as row counts or file names. Parameters are external inputs provided at runtime, commonly used for environment-specific values like server names, database names, or file paths.

A Full Load reloads all records every time the package runs, which is simple but inefficient for large datasets. Incremental Load processes only new or modified records, making it faster, more scalable, and the preferred approach in production environments.

In my project, SSIS was used to extract data from SQL Server and flat files, apply transformations such as Lookup and Derived Column, and load cleansed data into reporting tables. We implemented incremental loading, logging, and error handling to ensure reliable and efficient data processing for Power BI reporting.

SSIS is used because it provides a robust platform for ETL processes, supports multiple data sources, offers built-in transformations, and allows automation through scheduling. It helps organizations move and prepare data efficiently for reporting, analytics, and business intelligence solutions.

"Across both my SAR (Finance) and Inventory (Retail) projects, I was involved in the complete report development lifecycle — requirement gathering, stakeholder discussions, data modeling, dashboard development, testing, UAT support, deployment, and production support — not just building the report and handing it off. My documented flow is Source validation → SQL data-quality checks → Duplicate/NULL checks → KPI validation → Power BI/DAX validation → Report testing → UAT → Stakeholder sign-off → Production deployment → Post-deployment refresh validation."

UAT — How I Describe My Actual Approach

After internal testing and DAX validation, I moved the report to the UAT environment and worked directly with business users to validate KPIs and report functionality. Stakeholders reviewed numbers against their business expectations, gave feedback, and I resolved issues before getting sign-off. My documented UAT process includes:

  • Sample-data testing
  • DAX unit testing
  • Business-user KPI sign-off
  • Validation before production deployment

On the SAR project specifically, I partnered with Finance stakeholders during UAT to validate spend figures, budget calculations, security requirements (RLS), and dashboard usability.

On the Inventory project (DC allocation), I validated the 60/30/10 allocation-split logic against manual allocation sheets for two weeks before cutting over — a concrete example of UAT going beyond "does the number look right" into "does it hold up against a manual process the business already trusts."

Training — How I Describe It

I combine a short live walkthrough of the dashboard with a one-page quick-reference guide (what each visual means, how to filter it), plus a recorded video for anyone who misses the session. I also hold informal office hours in the first couple of weeks after launch, since most real questions only surface once people start using it on live data — not during the training session itself.

On the SAR project, this translated to assisting Finance and business users with dashboard navigation, security behavior, KPI interpretation, and self-service reporting capabilities.

After internal validation and DAX unit testing, I moved the report to the UAT environment and worked with business stakeholders to validate the numbers against their expectations. I resolved any data, calculation, or visualization issues raised, and confirmed final numbers matched agreed business definitions before getting sign-off for production deployment.

I validate in three layers: first, reconcile totals against the source system by comparing a raw SQL aggregate to the DAX measure for the same filter context; second, test edge cases — blank/null handling, filter context changes across visuals, totals vs. subtotals; third, a business-side pre-check — walking the SME through 2–3 known data points they can verify from memory before the dashboard formally goes live.

A short live walkthrough combined with a one-page quick-reference guide covering what each visual means and how to filter it, plus a recorded video for anyone who misses the session. I also hold informal office hours for the first couple of weeks post-launch, since real questions mostly come up once people are using it with live data.

I lead with business impact, not mechanism — for example "this DC is stocking out 30% more often than it should" before "because of an incorrect allocation weighting." I use visuals and concrete comparisons instead of jargon, and check understanding by asking them to restate the takeaway back to me.

I maintain a mapping document linking each report field/KPI back to its source table and the SQL logic/view that produces it — a single source of truth. So if a stakeholder questions a number, I trace it directly back to the source logic instead of re-deriving it from scratch, which is especially valuable during UAT.

Develop → Test/UAT → Publish → Configure Gateway & Refresh → Apply Security/RLS → Share with Users → Monitor Production. I've used Deployment Pipelines to promote a report from Dev, validate it in UAT, and only then push it to Production, rather than manually re-publishing files across workspaces.

I triage by business impact first — is this a wrong number stakeholders are actively using, or something cosmetic? For anything affecting decisions, I communicate the issue and expected fix timeline immediately, do root cause analysis rather than a surface patch, and add a validation check afterward so the same class of bug doesn't recur.

A Test Cases/UAT Document for validating calculations and getting business sign-off, and a User Guide/Knowledge Transfer document explaining dashboard navigation, filters, KPIs, and usage for end users.

Situation: On the Inventory Optimization & Allocation Analytics project, I proposed a revised allocation logic after identifying that DC1 was receiving more stock than its share of stores warranted (a 60/30/10 rebalancing recommendation).

Task: Before this change could go live, I needed the allocation team to trust the new logic wasn't going to make things worse.

Action: I validated the 60/30/10 split logic against the business's own manual allocation sheets for two weeks before cutting over — running it in parallel rather than asking for blind trust. During this UAT window, I walked stakeholders through the before/after numbers, led with the business impact ("stockouts drop, allocation matches actual store demand") rather than the SQL/DAX mechanics, and let them verify a few known data points themselves.

Result: The team signed off on the new allocation logic with confidence, it went to production, and it fed into a ~30% reduction in stockouts and ~10% improvement in allocation accuracy. After go-live, I also added a Last Refreshed indicator and a refresh-validation check, since a separate incident showed the report could silently keep serving stale allocation numbers if a Gateway refresh failed — a direct result of the "what if this breaks after UAT" thinking that UAT alone doesn't catch.

"SSRS is Microsoft's paginated reporting tool used for pixel-perfect operational reports such as invoices, statements, and scheduled reports. It uses data sources, datasets, parameters, subscriptions, and tablix controls to build reports. Compared to Power BI, SSRS focuses on formatted reporting and printing, while Power BI focuses on interactive analytics and dashboards. I've worked primarily with Power BI but understand SSRS architecture, paginated reports, subscriptions, report deployment, and its integration with Power BI Service."

SSRS (SQL Server Reporting Services) is Microsoft's reporting platform used to create, deploy, and manage paginated reports. It is mainly used for operational and pixel-perfect reports that can be exported to PDF, Excel, Word, or emailed automatically.

SSRSPower BI
Paginated reportsInteractive dashboards
Pixel-perfect formattingSelf-service analytics
Best for invoices, statementsBest for visual analysis
Scheduled delivery via subscriptionsSharing via Power BI Service
SQL Server basedCloud-first analytics platform

Interview line: "Power BI is used for analytics and visualization, whereas SSRS is preferred for highly formatted operational reports."

A paginated report is a report with fixed layouts where content fits exactly into pages when exported to PDF or printed.

Examples:

  • Invoice
  • Payslip
  • Bank Statement
  • Customer Report
  1. Report Designer
  2. Report Server
  3. Data Sources
  4. Datasets
  5. Report Builder
  6. Report Manager/Web Portal

Data Source — Connection information. Example: SQL Server connection.

Dataset — The actual query that retrieves data from the source.

SELECT * FROM Sales

A shared data source is a centrally managed database connection that can be reused across multiple reports.

Benefit: Easier maintenance and security management.

Parameters allow users to filter report data dynamically.

Example:

  • Start Date
  • End Date
  • Region
  • Product Category

Subscriptions automatically deliver reports through email or file shares on a schedule.

Example:

  • Daily Sales Report at 8 AM
  • Weekly Inventory Report every Monday

Standard Subscription — Fixed recipients and parameters.

Data-Driven Subscription — Recipients and parameters come from a database table.

A report snapshot stores report data at a specific point in time to improve performance and provide historical reporting.

Caching stores report data temporarily so repeated requests don't hit the database every time.

Benefit: Faster report performance.

  • PDF
  • Excel
  • Word
  • CSV
  • XML
  • TIFF

Tablix is the main data region in SSRS that combines features of both tables and matrices.

It supports:

  • Row Groups
  • Column Groups
  • Aggregations

Table — Fixed columns.

Matrix — Dynamic columns generated from data.

Example: Sales by Month → Matrix. Employee List → Table.

SSRS uses VB.NET expressions.

Example:

=Sum(Fields!SalesAmount.Value)
=Today()
  • Optimize SQL queries
