Say: It takes the current row's column values from the row context and uses them as filters for evaluating the expression.

Say: Filters operate at different scopes; report filters affect the whole report, page filters affect a page, visual filters affect a visual, and drill-through carries the selected context to a target page.

Say: ALL() removes filters from the specified table or column and is commonly used to calculate a total independent of that filter.

)

ALL() removes filters from the specified table or column entirely. ALLSELECTED() generally preserves the broader external selection while removing only the current visual-level context.

For example, if a user selects 2025 and 2026 in a slicer, ALL(Date) ignores that date filter completely, while ALLSELECTED(Date) respects the user's overall slicer selection while calculating relative to that selected set. A common use case is percentage of selected total.

Say: CALCULATE() evaluates an expression in a modified filter context and is one of the most important DAX functions for advanced measures.

Because this is the full three-way comparison version of the same RELATED()/RELATEDTABLE() distinction this topic explains.

Say: RELATED() pulls a single value from the "one" side of a relationship into the "many" side. RELATEDTABLE() does the reverse — it pulls a table of related rows from the "many" side when you're on the "one" side. LOOKUPVALUE() retrieves a value based on matching conditions without needing an existing relationship at all.

Real-life case: Used LOOKUPVALUE() to pull a target/budget value from a disconnected budget table based on Store and Month, since no relationship existed (or should exist) between that table and the main model.

Say: Yes — a model can contain multiple fact tables as long as they share common dimensions, since each fact table typically represents a different business process.

Real-life case: In my project, FactSales and FactInventory both connect to shared DimDate and DimProduct tables, letting me analyze sales and stock levels side by side.

Real-life case: On the SAR model, Actuals and Budget are separate fact tables sharing the same Date dimension — this is exactly the pattern I used so a Fiscal-YTD-vs-Prior-Year comparison lines up correctly across both, rather than one fact table's time intelligence silently drifting out of sync with the other's.

Say: Use VAR/RETURN for readability and to avoid re-evaluating the same expression twice, prefer measures over calculated columns where possible, avoid FILTER() over an entire large table when a simpler boolean filter argument works, keep all measures organized in a dedicated measure table, and format code consistently.

Real-life case: Refactored a long single-line measure into VAR-based steps, which made debugging a KPI's logic significantly faster when a stakeholder questioned a number.

Say: Iterators evaluate an expression row-by-row over a table then aggregate the result — AVERAGEX for row-level averages, COUNTX for conditional row counts, MINX/MAXX for row-level min/max, and FILTER() to build a filtered table for use inside CALCULATE or another iterator.

Real-life case: Used AVERAGEX to calculate average order value per transaction, rather than a flat average of an already-aggregated column, which would have given a mathematically different (and wrong) answer.

Say: HASONEVALUE() checks whether a column currently has exactly one distinct value in the filter context — used to avoid a misleading aggregate (like a "total" mislabeled as a single item) when multiple items are selected.

Query:

Store Name Display =
IF(
    HASONEVALUE(Store[StoreName]),
    VALUES(Store[StoreName]),
    "Multiple Stores"
)

Real-life case: Used this to show a store's name in a card visual only when a single store was selected, and "Multiple Stores" otherwise, instead of a blank or an arbitrary first value.

Say: VAR stores an intermediate calculation once so it isn't re-evaluated multiple times within the same expression, which improves both readability and performance; RETURN outputs the final result.

Query:

Stockout % =
VAR StockoutCount = CALCULATE(COUNTROWS(Inventory), Inventory[Stock] = 0)
VAR TotalCount = COUNTROWS(Inventory)
RETURN
    DIVIDE(StockoutCount, TotalCount)

Real-life case: Used VAR to calculate the stockout count once and reuse it in both the numerator and denominator of a stockout % measure, avoiding a duplicate, wasteful evaluation of the same filter.

Say: RELATED() pulls a single value from the "one" side of a relationship into the "many" side. RELATEDTABLE() does the reverse — it pulls a table of related rows from the "many" side when you're on the "one" side. LOOKUPVALUE() retrieves a value based on matching conditions without needing an existing relationship at all.

Real-life case: Used LOOKUPVALUE() to pull a target/budget value from a disconnected budget table based on Store and Month, since no relationship existed (or should exist) between that table and the main model.

Say: EXCEPT() returns the rows in one table that are not present in another — useful for finding items in one list but absent from a second.

Query:

Missing SKUs =
COUNTROWS(
    EXCEPT(
        VALUES(Catalog[SKU]),
        VALUES(AllocationFeed[SKU])
    )
)

Real-life case: Used EXCEPT() to find SKUs listed in the master catalog but missing from the current allocation feed — a fast gap-analysis check without a full reconciliation query.

Say: I filter the 30-day window down to only days with actual sales before averaging, so zero-sales days (like stockout days) don't silently dilute the average.

Query:

Avg Sales Excl Zero Days =
CALCULATE(
    AVERAGE(Sales[Amount]),
    DATESINPERIOD('Date'[Date], MAX('Date'[Date]), -30, DAY),
    Sales[Amount] > 0
)

Real-life case: Applied this pattern so a store's average daily sell-through wasn't understated just because it had a run of stockout days with zero recorded sales.

Say: Combine CALCULATE with TOPN() over ALL() of the dimension, ranked by the measure — this makes the Top N adjust dynamically with whatever filters/slicers are currently applied.

Query:

Top 5 Customer Sales =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    TOPN(5, ALL(Customer[Name]), [Total Sales], DESC)
)

Real-life case: Built a Top 5 Underperforming Stores measure using RANKX + TOPN that updated dynamically based on whichever date range was currently selected.

Because this is the same dynamic-Top-N pattern applied to Products instead of Customers — using RANKX + a disconnected parameter table instead of a fixed TOPN(5, ...).

Say: I create a What-If parameter or disconnected Top N table, rank products using the selected N, and filter the visual using the rank.

Query:

Product Rank =
RANKX(
    ALLSELECTED(Product[ProductName]),
    [Total Sales],
    ,
    DESC,
    DENSE
)

Show Top N =
IF(
    [Product Rank] <= SELECTEDVALUE('Top N'[Value]),
    1,
    0
)

Real-life case: Let management choose Top 5, Top 10, or Top 20 products from a slicer.

Say: I always use DIVIDE() instead of the / operator for any ratio measure, to avoid divide-by-zero errors surfacing as report errors.

Query:

Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Profit = [Sales] - SUM(Sales[Cost])
Margin % = DIVIDE([Profit], [Sales])
Growth % = DIVIDE([Sales] - [Sales PY], [Sales PY])
Variance = [Actual] - [Target]

Real-life case: Built this exact core measure set as the foundation of the SAR dashboard's KPI layer, with every downstream visual referencing these rather than re-deriving the logic per visual.

Calculated columns consume more storage/memory because they’re computed row-by-row at refresh time and physically stored in the VertiPaq compressed model, just like a regular column. Measures consume more runtime/CPU instead — they’re computed on the fly at query time in the current filter context and aren’t stored at all. So the trade-off is: calculated columns cost you model size, measures cost you query-time calculation.

No. Slicers filter based on column values that exist in the model — a measure returns a single dynamic scalar recalculated per context, so there’s nothing static to slice by. The workaround is a disconnected “parameter” table with static values, paired with SWITCH(SELECTEDVALUE(...)) logic in a measure, so the user is technically slicing a column on the parameter table, not the measure itself — that’s how I built dynamic measure selection.

Because this question shows the exact disconnected-table workaround referenced here — the practical solution to "measures can't be sliced directly."

Say: I create a small disconnected Metric table and a SWITCH() measure that returns the selected measure based on SELECTEDVALUE(), so one visual can show Revenue, Profit, or Quantity depending on the slicer.

Query:

Selected Metric =
SWITCH(
    SELECTEDVALUE(Metric[Metric]),
    "Revenue",[Revenue],
    "Profit",[Profit],
    "Quantity",[Quantity Sold]
)

Real-life case: On executive dashboards I've used this to let stakeholders flip between KPIs on the same chart instead of building four separate visuals.

Because every calculated column is materialized and stored per row in the compressed model — with millions of rows, that adds real memory overhead and slows down processing/refresh time. It also doesn’t benefit from context transition the way measures do. My rule of thumb: if a value needs to be used as a filter, slicer, or in RLS, it has to be a calculated column; anything purely for calculation and aggregation should be a measure instead.

I use a disconnected table listing measure names, then a single measure that switches between the real measures based on what’s selected in a slicer built off that disconnected table:

Selected Measure =
SWITCH(
    SELECTEDVALUE('Measure Selector'[MeasureName]),
    "Revenue", [Total Revenue],
    "Units", [Total Units],
    "Stockout %", [Stockout Rate],
    [Total Revenue]
)

This lets a stakeholder toggle KPIs on the same visual without me building duplicate charts.

This gives a trailing 12-month window that moves with whatever date is in context — I use this pattern for trend cards where stakeholders want to see momentum, not just the current period.

Rolling 12M Revenue =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Revenue],
    DATESINPERIOD('Date'[Date], MAX('Date'[Date]), -12, MONTH)
)

Because this uses the exact same DATESINPERIOD() trailing-window pattern, just with a 30-day window instead of 12 months.

Rolling sales calculates sales over a moving window, such as the last 7, 30 or 90 days.

Rolling 30 Days =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    DATESINPERIOD(
        'Date'[Date],
        MAX('Date'[Date]),
        -30,
        DAY
    )
)

In DAX:

7-Day Moving Avg =
AVERAGEX(
    DATESINPERIOD('Date'[Date], MAX('Date'[Date]), -7, DAY),
    [Total Revenue]
)

In SQL, using a window function instead of a self-join:

SELECT
    OrderDate,
    Revenue,
    AVG(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS MovingAvg7Day
FROM Sales;

Same concept in both — a defined trailing window recalculated per row — DAX does it via a virtual date table filter, SQL does it via the ROWS BETWEEN frame clause.

WITH DailyCategorySales AS (
    SELECT SaleDate, CategoryID, SUM(SalesAmount) AS DailySales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY SaleDate, CategoryID
),
RollingSales AS (
    SELECT
        CategoryID, SaleDate,
        AVG(DailySales) OVER (
            PARTITION BY CategoryID ORDER BY SaleDate
            ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) AS Rolling30DayAvg
    FROM DailyCategorySales
)
SELECT TOP 5 CategoryID, Rolling30DayAvg
FROM RollingSales
WHERE SaleDate = (SELECT MAX(SaleDate) FROM RollingSales)
ORDER BY Rolling30DayAvg DESC;

I aggregate sales to the category-and-day level, calculate a 30-day rolling average using AVG() OVER(), then take the latest available rolling average for each category and return the top five.

30-second answer: Running sales means cumulative sales from the beginning of the selected period up to the current date. I typically calculate it using CALCULATE with ALLSELECTED or a suitable date filter.

Example:

Running Sales =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    FILTER(
        ALLSELECTED('Date'[Date]),
        'Date'[Date] <= MAX('Date'[Date])
    )
)

Where used? Trend analysis.

Example:

  • January → ₹10L
  • February → ₹18L cumulative
  • March → ₹27L cumulative

30-Second Explanation: Visual-level filters apply only to a single visual. They do not affect other charts or tables on the page. We use them when a specific visual needs to show only a subset of data.

Real-Life Example: In a Sales Dashboard, you have a chart showing only Top 10 Products by Revenue, while other visuals show all products. The filter is applied only to that chart.

30-Second Explanation: Page-level filters affect all visuals on a single report page. Any visual placed on that page follows the same filter condition.

Real-Life Example: A regional sales page is filtered to India region only. Every KPI, chart, and table on that page displays Indian sales data.

30-Second Explanation: Report-level filters affect every page and visual in the entire report. They provide a common filter across all report pages.

Real-Life Example: A company wants managers to see only Current Financial Year (FY2026) data. A report-level filter is applied so all pages show FY2026 information.

30-Second Explanation: Drillthrough filters pass selected data from one page to another for detailed analysis. Users can right-click a data point and navigate to a detailed page.

Real-Life Example: A manager sees low sales for Store 101 and drills through to a detailed page showing product-wise sales, inventory, and customer metrics for that store.

30-Second Explanation: Slicers are interactive filters placed on the report canvas. Users can dynamically filter data without opening the filter pane.

Real-Life Example: Users select Year = 2026 or Region = South from slicers, and all connected visuals update instantly.

30-Second Explanation: When a user clicks a data point in one visual, other visuals automatically filter or highlight related data.

Real-Life Example: Clicking Electronics Category in a pie chart filters all sales, profit, and customer visuals to show only Electronics data.

30-Second Explanation: Relative date filters automatically show data based on time periods like last 7 days, last month, or last year.

Real-Life Example: An operations dashboard always displays Last 30 Days Orders without manual date updates.

Interview Answer (Most Asked): "Power BI provides Visual-Level Filters, Page-Level Filters, Report-Level Filters, Drillthrough Filters, Slicers, Cross-Filtering/Cross-Highlighting, and Relative Date Filters. Visual filters affect one visual, page filters affect all visuals on a page, report filters affect the entire report, and slicers allow users to interactively filter data. In real projects, we commonly use page filters for region-wise dashboards, report filters for financial year restrictions, and slicers for user-driven analysis."

This improves both usability and performance."

Answer (30 sec): "I use business-friendly labels instead of technical names, place KPIs at the top, use clear titles, consistent color coding, and tooltips for explanations. I also limit the number of visuals per page and design the report so users can understand it without training."

Answer (30 sec): "In Excel, I create a Pivot Table from the source data and then insert a Pivot Chart. The chart automatically updates when the Pivot Table changes. I can also add slicers and timelines so users can dynamically filter data and see real-time chart updates."

Answer (30 sec): "For real-time dashboards, I use streaming or DirectQuery datasets and focus only on critical KPIs. I minimize complex calculations, use cards, gauges, and trend charts, and configure automatic refresh. The design prioritizes speed and quick decision-making."

Answer (30 sec): "I validate source data, check row counts, verify KPI calculations with business users, test filters and relationships, and compare report results with source systems. I also perform UAT testing and ensure there are no duplicate or missing records before publishing."

Because this question breaks the "verify KPI calculations" step mentioned here into the actual three-layer validation process used before UAT.

I validate in three layers: first, reconcile totals against the source system by comparing a raw SQL aggregate to the DAX measure for the same filter context; second, test edge cases — blank/null handling, filter context changes across visuals, totals vs. subtotals; third, a business-side pre-check — walking the SME through 2–3 known data points they can verify from memory before the dashboard formally goes live.

Because this question gives a concrete, high-volume scenario version of the same slow-report troubleshooting.

Aggregation tables at a coarser grain for the visuals that don't need row-level detail, strict star schema with single-direction relationships, incremental refresh, removing unused/high-cardinality columns, and disabling Auto Date/Time (it silently creates a hidden date table per date column, which is expensive at scale). If none of that is enough, I'd consider a composite model — aggregated Import layer with DirectQuery only for drill-through detail.

I open Performance Analyzer first — it breaks down time spent per visual into DAX query time vs. visual rendering time vs. other. If one or two visuals dominate, I look at their DAX (usually a non-optimized measure, unnecessary bidirectional filter, or too many nested CALCULATEs). If it's spread evenly across many visuals, it's more likely a model-level issue — too many visuals on one page, high-cardinality columns, or unnecessary calculated columns bloating the model. I always isolate the bottleneck with data before touching anything.

Answer (30 sec): "I balance UX and performance by showing only the most important visuals on the main page and using drill-through, bookmarks, and tooltips for detailed analysis. I also optimize DAX, reduce visual interactions, and avoid loading unnecessary data to maintain a smooth user experience."

Say: Power Query is Power BI's data ingestion and transformation engine used to connect, clean, reshape, combine, and prepare data before it enters the semantic model.

Say: Duplicate creates an independent copy of the query steps, while Reference creates a new query that starts from the output of the referenced query.

Real-life case: I use Reference when several downstream queries should reuse a common cleaned source.

Because this question expands the same distinction into a concrete staging-architecture scenario with a clear "when to use each" answer.

30-second explanation: When I duplicate a query, Power Query creates an independent copy of the query and its transformation steps. Changes to the original query don't automatically affect the duplicate. With Reference, the new query uses the output of the original query, so changes to the base query flow into the referenced query.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose I have one Sales Staging query and need Sales, Returns and High-Value Sales tables. I would create one staging query and Reference it three times. This avoids repeating the source extraction and common cleaning steps. I would use Duplicate when I need a completely independent transformation path.

Say: Yes; I can use Conditional Columns for simple logic and M expressions or custom functions for more complex multi-condition transformations.

= Table.AddColumn(
    Source,
    "Risk",
    each if [WOC] < 5 then "Red"
         else if [WOC] <= 12 then "Amber"
         else "Green"
)

Real-life case: Classify Weeks of Cover into Red, Amber, and Green inventory-risk bands.

Say: I create a conditional column based on the time portion of the datetime and assign each interval to a shift.

Query:

= Table.AddColumn(
    Source,
    "Shift",
    each
        if Time.From([DateTime]) >= #time(6,0,0)
           and Time.From([DateTime]) < #time(14,0,0)
        then "Morning"
        else if Time.From([DateTime]) >= #time(14,0,0)
           and Time.From([DateTime]) < #time(22,0,0)
        then "Evening"
        else "Night"
)

Real-life case: Categorize transactions or operational events into three business shifts.

Say: I split the email at @ or use Text.BeforeDelimiter() to return the username.

Say: I can use StartDate and EndDate parameters in Power Query to generate a dynamic list of dates and convert it into a Date table.

Query:

let
    StartDate = #date(2024, 1, 1),
    EndDate = #date(2026, 12, 31),
    Dates = List.Dates(
        StartDate,
        Duration.Days(EndDate - StartDate) + 1,
        #duration(1, 0, 0, 0)
    ),
    Calendar = Table.FromList(
        Dates,
        Splitter.SplitByNothing(),
        {"Date"}
    )
in
    Calendar

Real-life case: Parameters allow the calendar range to be changed without rewriting the transformation.

Say: try...otherwise catches an error at the step level and replaces it with a fallback value instead of letting the whole refresh fail.

try [Sales]/[Qty]
otherwise 0

30-second explanation: In Power Query, null values and conversion errors can cause problems during transformations. I can use try to attempt an operation and otherwise to provide a fallback value if an error occurs. This is particularly useful when source data is inconsistent.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose an Amount column contains a mix of valid numbers and text like "N/A" or "Unknown". Instead of allowing the query to fail, I can use:

Table.AddColumn(

30-second answer: "Power Query is mainly used for data extraction and transformation before the data enters the model. DAX is used for calculations and analytical logic after the data is loaded into the model. Tabular Editor is primarily a modeling and development tool used to manage semantic models, calculation groups, advanced measures and metadata more efficiently. So I generally use Power Query for ETL, DAX for analytics and Tabular Editor for advanced model management."

Simple memory trick: Power Query → Prepare data. DAX → Calculate data. Tabular Editor → Manage/model data.

Real-life case: Suppose source data has a date stored as 20260819. I'd transform the date format in Power Query, then calculate Total Sales = SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) using DAX, then manage hundreds of measures or calculation groups using Tabular Editor.

Power BI Dataflow is a cloud-based ETL tool used to extract, clean, transform, and prepare data using Power Query Online. It allows us to centralize data preparation logic instead of repeating the same transformations in every report.

For example, if multiple reports need the same Customer, Product, or Sales data, we can create a dataflow once, apply all required transformations, and then allow multiple semantic models to consume that prepared data. This improves consistency, reusability, and maintenance.

Interview answer: "In my projects, I would use Power BI Dataflows as a centralized data preparation layer. I can connect to different sources, perform transformations using Power Query, schedule refreshes, and make the cleaned entities available to multiple semantic models and reports. This helps avoid duplicate ETL logic and provides a more governed and reusable architecture."

Dataflow is the ETL layer, where we connect to sources and clean and transform data. Semantic model is the modeling and business-logic layer, where we create relationships, measures, and calculations. Multiple semantic models or reports can consume prepared data from a dataflow, while multiple reports can also connect to the same semantic model. So, simply, Dataflow prepares the data, Semantic Model organizes and calculates the data for reporting.

Say: Append combines rows from two or more tables with compatible structures.

Real-life case: Combine January, February, and March transaction tables into one fact table.

Say: Merge joins two queries using one or more matching columns and adds columns from the related query.

Real-life case: Merge a Sales table with a Product lookup using ProductID to bring Category and Brand.

Say: Append adds rows vertically; Merge combines related columns horizontally based on matching keys.

Real-life case: Monthly files are appended; Product attributes are merged into sales data.

Because this question gives the same Append vs Merge distinction with a SQL-analogy memory trick and a concrete two-table example.

30-second explanation: Merge combines tables horizontally using matching keys, similar to a SQL JOIN. Append combines tables vertically by stacking rows from one table below another. I use Merge when I need additional columns and Append when I have similar datasets from different sources or periods.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose I have a Customers table and an Orders table sharing a CustomerID key — I would Merge using CustomerID to bring customer information into Orders. If I have monthly sales files (Sales_Jan, Sales_Feb, Sales_Mar) with the same structure, I would Append them.

Interview line: "Merge is like a JOIN; Append is like UNION ALL."

Say: Power Query's Merge supports six join kinds: Left Outer, Right Outer, Full Outer, Inner, Left Anti, and Right Anti — the anti joins return only the non-matching rows from one side.

Real-life case: I've used Left Anti to find records in a source table that have no match in a reference table — for example transactions with a ProductID that doesn't exist in the Product dimension, which is a useful data-quality check.

Say: I'd use "Merge Columns" from the UI for a simple concatenation with a chosen separator, or write a Custom Column with M like Text.Combine({[Col1],[Col2]}, " ") for more control over formatting.

= Text.Combine({[FirstName], [LastName]}, " ")

Real-life case: I use the Custom Column/M approach whenever I need conditional formatting or handling of nulls within the concatenation, since the UI-only "Merge Columns" option is more limited.

Say: Yes — nested if...then...else in a Custom Column for multi-condition logic, the Conditional Column UI for simpler cases, or full M code in the Advanced Editor for anything more complex than the UI can express.

= if [SalesVolume] > 100000 then "High"

  else "Normal"

Real-life case: Used nested conditional logic to classify records into priority tiers based on more than one input column, rather than building several separate conditional columns and combining them afterward.

Say: Duplicate creates an independent copy of a query — changes to the source afterward don't propagate to it. Reference creates a query that depends on the original, so upstream changes flow through automatically, and it's more efficient since it doesn't reload the source data separately.

Real-life case: I use Reference queries to build staged "cleaned" and "final" layers on top of one raw source query, rather than duplicating and reloading the source at every stage.

Say: Conditional Column is UI-based for simple if/then rules without writing code; Custom Column uses the M formula language and supports more complex logic, calculations, and nested conditions the UI can't express.

Real-life case: Used a Custom Column with M code to calculate a weighted score combining multiple input factors — something the Conditional Column UI genuinely can't do in one step.

Say: M is the functional query language behind Power Query — every UI transformation step generates M code, viewable and editable in the Advanced Editor, which lets me write custom logic beyond what the UI exposes.

Real-life case: Edited M code directly in the Advanced Editor to add try...otherwise error-handling around a source that occasionally had schema changes, which isn't something the step-by-step UI can add on its own.

Say: Query folding is Power Query's ability to translate supported transformation steps into native source queries so the source performs the work.

Real-life case: A filter applied to a SQL Server table can be translated into a SQL WHERE clause instead of importing all rows first.

Say: It reduces data transferred to Power BI and lets the source database use its processing and indexing capabilities.

Real-life case: Folding is especially valuable when working with large SQL Server fact tables.

Say: It pushes supported transformations to the source, reducing network transfer, local processing, and the amount of data Power BI needs to load.

Real-life case: Filtering a 100M-row source table at SQL Server is preferable to importing all 100M rows and filtering afterward.

Say: Power Query translates compatible M transformations into the source's native query language, such as SQL for SQL Server.

Real-life case: A Power Query filter can become a SQL WHERE predicate at the source.

Say: It depends on the connector, but examples can include unsupported custom M logic, certain row-by-row transformations, and operations that the source cannot translate.

Real-life case: I verify the actual folding behavior instead of assuming a particular step always breaks folding.

Because this question walks through what to actually do once one of these folding-breaking operations is found, including a concrete step-flow diagram.

30-second explanation: First, I identify exactly which transformation broke folding. I would check the query steps and use View Native Query where available. Then I would see whether the transformation can be replaced with a foldable operation or moved later in the query. If possible, I would push the transformation into SQL Server or another source system.

Source
   ↓
Filter Rows        ← Folding works
   ↓
Select Columns      ← Folding works
   ↓
Custom M Column      ← Folding breaks
   ↓
Merge

I would first check whether the custom M logic can be rewritten using a native/foldable transformation. If it cannot, I would move that custom transformation later, after filtering and reducing the dataset.

Say: I filter and select required columns early, preserve foldable steps, avoid unnecessary custom transformations before source-side filtering, and verify folding during development.

Real-life case: For a large SQL fact table, I push date and business filters to SQL Server before loading the model.

Say: Yes — with SQL Server sources folding works well since Power Query can translate filters and joins into SQL. Excel and CSV sources don't support query folding at all, because there's no query engine on the other end to push logic into — Power Query has to load the file and process every step locally.

Real-life case: For Excel-based sources, keeping the file small and filtering early in Excel itself matters more than step ordering, since there's no source-side engine to fold into.

Say: I check by right-clicking a step and seeing if "View Native Query" is available — if it's greyed out, folding has broken at that step. For mixed scenarios, I reorder steps so all foldable operations (filters, column selection, basic type changes) happen first, and push non-foldable custom logic to the end, so the source still does as much filtering as possible before the non-folding steps run.

Real-life case: On the SAR project I caught a broken fold this way — a custom column placed early was silently forcing every downstream step to run locally, so I moved it to the end of the query and folding resumed.

Say: Yes; parameters can make source paths, date ranges, environments, and transformation logic configurable without rewriting the query.

ETL: Extract → Transform → Load. Transformation occurs before loading into the target.

ELT: Extract → Load → Transform. Data is loaded first and transformed using the target platform.

30-second answer: "ETL transforms data before loading it into the target system, while ELT loads the raw data first and performs transformations inside the target platform. In a modern cloud architecture, ELT is common because cloud warehouses and lakehouses provide scalable compute. For example, I could ingest retail sales data into a lakehouse, transform it using SQL or Spark, create curated tables and then connect Power BI to the semantic model."

Pipeline example:

Source Systems → ADF / Fabric Pipeline → Data Lake / Lakehouse → Transform → Curated Tables → Power BI Semantic Model → Reports

Real-life case: "For a retail organization, daily sales from multiple stores can be ingested into a lakehouse, transformed into curated fact and dimension tables and then consumed by Power BI."

30-second explanation: In Power Query M, let is used to define a sequence of transformation steps, and in specifies which final step should be returned. Each step can use the output of the previous step. This makes M code easy to read and debug because every transformation has a name.

30-second real-case solution: For example, if I receive a sales table, I can first filter the rows, then remove unnecessary columns, and finally return the cleaned table. I would structure it using let and in so each transformation is clearly separated.

let
    Source = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Sales"]}[Content],
    FilteredRows = Table.SelectRows(Source, each [Sales] > 10000),
    RemovedColumns = Table.RemoveColumns(FilteredRows, {"Comments"})
in
    RemovedColumns

Interview line: "let defines the transformation steps, and in returns the final output."

30-second explanation: M and DAX serve different purposes. M is used in Power Query for data extraction, cleaning and transformation before the data enters the model. DAX is used after the data is loaded for calculations, measures and analytical logic. I prefer M for static transformations and DAX for calculations that need to respond dynamically to filter context. M performs transformations before loading, while DAX performs calculations on loaded data.

30-second real-case solution: For example, if I need to remove duplicates, clean customer names or create a fixed category based on sales, I would use Power Query/M. But if I need Total Sales, YTD Sales, YoY Growth or Sales % of Total, I would use DAX because these calculations need to respond to slicers and filters.

Interview line: "M prepares the data; DAX analyzes the data."

30-second explanation: Query folding occurs when Power Query translates transformations into queries that are executed by the source system instead of processing everything inside Power BI. For example, when connecting to SQL Server, a filter can be pushed back to SQL Server. This reduces data transfer and improves refresh performance.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose SQL Server has 100 million sales rows, but my report needs only the last two years. I would apply the date filter as early as possible and use transformations that support folding. I would check View Native Query where available and avoid unnecessary non-foldable transformations early in the query.

Interview line: "I preserve query folding by filtering early, minimizing non-foldable steps and pushing transformations to the source whenever possible."

30-second explanation: I would troubleshoot systematically rather than immediately blaming Power BI. First, I would check the source query and data volume. Then I would check whether query folding is working, whether unnecessary columns and rows are being loaded, and whether there are expensive transformation steps. I would also review joins, data types and the number of applied steps. My approach: filter at source, remove unnecessary columns, minimize transformation steps and maintain query folding.

30-second real-case solution: For example, if a SQL table has 50 million rows, I would first filter it to the required date range, select only required columns, and ensure the filter folds back to SQL Server. Then I would review joins and transformations. If the source is still slow, I would ask the database team about indexes or pre-aggregated views.

Interview line: "My first focus is reducing the amount of data entering Power Query."

30-second explanation: When I duplicate a query, Power Query creates an independent copy of the query and its transformation steps. Changes to the original query don't automatically affect the duplicate. With Reference, the new query uses the output of the original query, so changes to the base query flow into the referenced query.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose I have one Sales Staging query and need Sales, Returns and High-Value Sales tables. I would create one staging query and Reference it three times. This avoids repeating the source extraction and common cleaning steps. I would use Duplicate when I need a completely independent transformation path.

Interview line: "I prefer Reference for staging architecture and Duplicate when I need an independent copy."

30-second explanation: Table.SelectRows is used to filter rows from a table based on a condition. The each keyword defines the condition evaluated for each row. It is one of the most commonly used M functions for filtering data.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose my business requirement is to analyze only West-region sales above ₹50,000. I can write:

FilteredRows =
    Table.SelectRows(
        Source,
        each [Region] = "West" and [Sales] > 50000
    )

For a single condition:

Table.SelectRows(Source, each [Sales] > 10000)

Interview line: "Table.SelectRows filters the input table based on a row-level condition."

30-second explanation: Table.AddColumn creates a new column based on an expression evaluated for every row. For multiple business conditions, I can use if...then...else statements. This is useful when the transformation is a fixed business rule — conditional columns and nested if statements for multiple conditions.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose the business wants to classify products based on sales:

Table.AddColumn(
    Source,
    "Sales Category",
    each
        if [Sales] >= 100000 then "High"
        else if [Sales] >= 50000 then "Medium"
        else "Low"
)

So: ₹100K+ → High, ₹50K–₹99K → Medium, Below ₹50K → Low.

Interview line: "I use Table.AddColumn with conditional logic when I need a row-level derived field during data preparation."

30-second explanation: In Power Query, null values and conversion errors can cause problems during transformations. I can use try to attempt an operation and otherwise to provide a fallback value if an error occurs. This is particularly useful when source data is inconsistent.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose an Amount column contains a mix of valid numbers and text like "N/A" or "Unknown". Instead of allowing the query to fail, I can use:

Table.AddColumn(
    Source,

    each try Number.From([Amount]) otherwise 0,

)

For null replacement:

Table.ReplaceValue(

30-second explanation: I use Power Query's text functions to standardize inconsistent source data. Text.Trim removes leading and trailing spaces, Text.Clean removes non-printable characters, and Text.Upper standardizes capitalization. I usually perform these transformations before joins or creating dimensions because inconsistent text can cause matching problems.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose customer names arrive inconsistently formatted with extra spaces and mixed casing. I can standardize them:

Table.TransformColumns(
    Source,
    {
        {
            "CustomerName",
            each Text.Upper(Text.Trim(Text.Clean(_))),
            type text
        }
    }
)

All values become consistently formatted.

Interview line: "I clean and standardize text before joins because inconsistent text can create incorrect matches."

30-second explanation: First, I identify the different date formats in the source. If the format is consistent, I change the column type to Date. If formats differ based on locale, I use Change Type → Using Locale or functions such as Date.FromText. If the column contains multiple formats, I use conditional logic to parse them safely. I avoid relying on automatic date detection when source formats are inconsistent.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose a source provides dates in DD/MM/YYYY format. I would explicitly apply the correct locale rather than allowing Power Query to guess:

Date.FromText([DateText], "en-GB")

Then I would validate the resulting Date column before loading it.

Interview line: "I avoid relying on automatic date detection when source formats are inconsistent; I explicitly control the locale."

30-second explanation: Merge combines tables horizontally using matching keys, similar to a SQL JOIN. Append combines tables vertically by stacking rows from one table below another. I use Merge when I need additional columns and Append when I have similar datasets from different sources or periods.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose I have a Customers table and an Orders table sharing a CustomerID key — I would Merge using CustomerID to bring customer information into Orders. If I have monthly sales files (Sales_Jan, Sales_Feb, Sales_Mar) with the same structure, I would Append them.

30-second explanation: A custom function allows me to write transformation logic once and reuse it for multiple inputs. It is particularly useful when the same transformation needs to be applied to many files, tables or columns. This improves maintainability and avoids duplicating M code.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose I receive multiple files and need to clean a Customer Name column in every file. I can create:

(CustomerName as text) as text =>
    Text.Upper(Text.Trim(CustomerName))

Then call it: CleanName([CustomerName]). For a folder containing hundreds of files, I can create a function that accepts each file's binary/table and applies the same transformation.

Interview line: "I use custom functions when the same transformation logic needs to be reused across multiple inputs."

30-second explanation: For recurring files such as monthly sales files, I use Folder.Files() to retrieve the files from a folder and then filter only the required files. I apply a common transformation function to each file and combine the resulting tables. This means new files can automatically be included during refresh.

30-second real-case solution: Instead of importing every monthly file individually, I would: Folder → Filter files → Transform each file → Combine → Load. Conceptually:

Source = Folder.Files("C:\Sales"),
FilteredFiles =
    Table.SelectRows(
        Source,
        each Text.EndsWith([Extension], ".xlsx")
    )

Then I would invoke a transformation function on each file and combine the resulting tables. Real-world benefit: when a new file is added to the folder, it can be picked up automatically on refresh.

30-second explanation: For large datasets, my first priority is reducing the amount of data processed. I filter rows and remove unnecessary columns as early as possible, preserve query folding, avoid expensive transformations, and push processing to the source where possible. I also review joins and data types because inefficient transformations can significantly increase refresh time.

30-second real-case solution: Suppose SQL Server contains 100 million sales records, but the report needs only the last three years and 10 columns. I would filter the date at source, select only required columns, preserve query folding, perform joins efficiently, avoid unnecessary custom transformations, and consider incremental refresh for historical data.

Interview line: "I optimize Power Query by reducing data volume first, then optimizing transformations."

30-second explanation: First, I identify exactly which transformation broke folding. I would check the query steps and use View Native Query where available. Then I would see whether the transformation can be replaced with a foldable operation or moved later in the query. If possible, I would push the transformation into SQL Server or another source system — identify the step that breaks folding, push transformations to the source, filter early and avoid custom columns too early.

30-second real-case solution:

Source
   ↓
Filter Rows        ← Folding works
   ↓
Select Columns      ← Folding works
   ↓
Custom M Column      ← Folding breaks
   ↓
Merge

I would first check whether the custom M logic can be rewritten using a native/foldable transformation. If it cannot, I would move that custom transformation later, after filtering and reducing the dataset. If the transformation is computationally heavy, I might move the logic to SQL:

SELECT
    *,
    CASE
        WHEN Sales >= 100000 THEN 'High'
        ELSE 'Low'
    END AS SalesCategory
FROM Sales

Then Power Query receives the already-transformed result.

Say: A star schema has a central fact table connected directly to denormalized dimension tables.

Say: A Semantic Model in Power BI is a centralized data model published to Power BI Service that contains tables, relationships, measures, hierarchies, and business logic. It acts as a single source of truth for the organization. Multiple reports can connect to the same semantic model, ensuring consistent KPIs and calculations across all dashboards while reducing duplication and maintenance effort.

Real-life case: In my retail project, Sales, Inventory, and Executive dashboards were all built on the same semantic model. When a measure like Profit Margin was updated in the model, the change automatically reflected across all reports without modifying each report individually.

Say: A fact table stores business events or measurements at a defined grain, such as sales transactions or inventory snapshots.

Real-life case: FactSales can contain ProductID, StoreID, DateID, UnitsSold, and Revenue.

Say: A dimension table stores descriptive attributes used to filter, group, and analyze facts.

Real-life case: Product contains SKU, Category, Brand, and Sourcing Country.

Say: Star schema provides clear relationships, simpler DAX, better usability, and efficient filter propagation.

Real-life case: A clean Product → FactSales relationship makes category and SKU analysis easier.

Because this expands the same recommendation into a deeper technical explanation (VertiPaq join paths) plus a concrete example.

OLTP/normalized schemas are optimized for transactional integrity — lots of joins, third normal form, minimal redundancy. That's the wrong shape for analytics. Star schema denormalizes into a central fact table surrounded by dimension tables, which gives VertiPaq fewer, simpler join paths to resolve, so DAX queries are faster and filter propagation is predictable — one hop from dimension to fact instead of chaining through multiple normalized tables. It's also easier for business users to understand: a Date, Product, and DC dimension around a Shipments fact table maps directly to how they think about the business, versus an ERD with 15 linked tables.

Say: It reduces unnecessary joins, keeps relationships simple, and works efficiently with Power BI's columnar storage engine.

Real-life case: A narrow fact table plus descriptive dimensions is easier to optimize than one large flattened table.

Say: A snowflake schema further normalizes dimensions into multiple related tables.

Real-life case: Product may connect to Subcategory, which connects to Category, instead of keeping those attributes in one Product dimension.

Say: Star keeps dimensions relatively denormalized and simple; Snowflake normalizes dimensions into additional related tables.

Real-life case: For Power BI reporting, I generally prefer Star unless normalization has a clear modeling benefit.

Say: Additional dimension joins and more complex filter paths can increase model complexity and query work.

Real-life case: I avoid unnecessary snowflaking in a semantic model when a simple dimension can provide the required attributes.

Say: Grain defines the lowest level of detail stored in a fact table — it answers "one row represents what?" and has to be decided before the fact table is even built.

Real-life case: In a retail FactSales table, the grain is one row per product, per store, per date, so a single row always represents exactly one product sold in one store on one day.

Say: A factless fact table records that an event occurred without storing any measures or numeric values — it exists purely to track occurrences, not amounts.

Real-life case: A StorePromotionParticipation table with only StoreID, PromotionID, and Date (no Sales Amount or Quantity) tracks which stores took part in a campaign.

Say: SCD defines how a dimension table handles changes to its attributes over time, and whether history should be preserved or simply overwritten.

Real-life case: When a customer's city changes from Pune to Mumbai, SCD logic decides whether I just update the record or keep both values for historical reporting.

Say: SCD Type 1 overwrites the old attribute value with the new one, so no history is maintained.

Real-life case: A customer's City column is simply updated from Pune to Mumbai, and the earlier value is lost — fine when the business only cares about the current state.

Say: SCD Type 2 inserts a new row whenever a tracked attribute changes, using StartDate/EndDate (or a current-record flag) to preserve full history.

Real-life case: When a customer moves from Pune to Mumbai, I'd insert a new row for Mumbai and close out the Pune row with an EndDate, so trend reports before and after the move stay accurate.

Say: Yes — a model can contain multiple fact tables as long as they share common dimensions, since each fact table typically represents a different business process.

Real-life case: In my project, FactSales and FactInventory both connect to shared DimDate and DimProduct tables, letting me analyze sales and stock levels side by side.

Say: I'd build one central FactSales table holding keys and metrics like Quantity and Revenue, surrounded by DimDate, DimProduct, DimStore, and DimCustomer tables holding descriptive attributes.

Real-life case: This is the same structure I used for the DC allocation project — FactSales connected to DimDate, DimStore, DimProduct, and DimCustomer, which kept the model fast and easy to filter.

Say: Modeling: star schema over snowflake, single-direction relationships unless a real scenario needs bidirectional, and measures instead of calculated columns wherever possible. Visualization: keep each page focused on one decision, use consistent color/KPI conventions, and avoid overloading a single page with too many visuals. Transformation: keep Power Query minimal and folding-friendly, and push heavy logic into SQL views for performance and auditability.

Real-life case: On the SAR project I kept currency conversion and heavy joins in SQL views, used Power Query only for final shaping, and built a star schema so DAX measures stayed simple and fast.

Say: Source/SQL: best for heavy logic like currency conversion — auditable, performant, reusable across reports, but changes need a deployment/DBA involvement. Power Query: good for lighter shaping close to the report, but can break folding and slow refresh if overused. DAX: best for logic that must respond dynamically to user filters/slicers, but it's the most expensive layer computationally if the underlying rule is static.

Real-life case: On the SAR project I put currency conversion in SQL specifically because it's a static, performance-sensitive rule, not something that needs to change per user interaction.

Say: The main cardinalities are one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many.

Real-life case: Product dimension to FactSales is typically one-to-many.

Say: Bi-directional filtering can create ambiguous filter paths, unexpected results, and unnecessary query complexity, so I prefer single-direction relationships unless there is a clear requirement.

Real-life case: In a star schema, dimensions normally filter facts in one direction.

Because this expands the same caution into a real project rule — bidirectional filtering kept to exactly one bridge table.

Single direction means filters flow only from the "one" side (dimension) to the "many" side (fact) — the standard star schema pattern. Both/bidirectional lets filters flow both ways, so filtering the fact table can also filter the dimension. I use bidirectional sparingly — mainly for many-to-many bridge tables — because it can create ambiguous filter paths and hurt performance. In my model I kept dimension-to-fact relationships single-direction and only turned on bidirectional filtering on the one bridge table I needed for a many-to-many product-to-region mapping.

Say: An active relationship is used automatically by the model, while an inactive relationship is available for specific calculations and can be activated with USERELATIONSHIP().

Query:

Sales by Ship Date =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    USERELATIONSHIP(
        Sales[ShipDate],
        'Date'[Date]
    )
)

Real-life case: Use Order Date as the active relationship and Ship Date as an inactive relationship when a fact table contains multiple dates.

Yes — Power BI allows multiple relationships between two tables, but only one can be active at a time; the rest are inactive. A common case is a fact table with both an Order Date and a Ship Date, both relating to the same Date dimension. The Order Date relationship is active by default; to use Ship Date in a calculation I activate it explicitly with USERELATIONSHIP() inside a CALCULATE(), rather than making it the default active path.

Say: I avoid unnecessary high-cardinality fields in the model, remove unused columns, use appropriate data types, and keep high-cardinality attributes out of visuals unless required.

Say: I prefer a bridge table with unique keys on the bridge side and one-to-many relationships from the bridge to the participating tables.

Real-life case: A Customer can belong to multiple Segments, so a CustomerSegment bridge can model the relationship cleanly.

Say: Single Direction: Filters flow in one direction (recommended, better performance). Bi-Directional: Filters flow both ways, useful in limited scenarios but may create ambiguity and slow performance.

Say: Bi-Directional Filtering allows filters to flow in both directions between tables. Avoid it unless required because it may create ambiguity, circular filtering, incorrect results, and slower performance.

Say: It occurs when multiple rows in one table can relate to multiple rows in another table.

Real-life case: A customer can belong to multiple groups and a group can contain multiple customers.

CustomerID | SegmentID

101        | A

Say: I create a bridge with unique relationship combinations and connect it to the dimensions using one-to-many relationships wherever possible.

Real-life case: This gives clearer filter propagation than directly creating an ambiguous many-to-many relationship between dimensions.

Say: Relationship direction controls how filters propagate between related tables; single direction is usually preferred in a star schema.

Real-life case: Product filters FactSales, but FactSales normally does not filter Product.

Say: CROSSFILTER() temporarily changes relationship cross-filter direction or disables a relationship during a specific calculation.

Query:

Sales by Customer =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    CROSSFILTER(
        Customer[CustomerID],
        Sales[CustomerID],
        BOTH
    )
)

Real-life case: Use it only when a specific calculation needs a temporary relationship-direction change.

Say: TREATAS() applies values from one table expression as filters to columns in another unrelated or differently related table.

Query:

Sales for Selected Products =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    TREATAS(
        VALUES(ProductSelector[ProductID]),
        Product[ProductID]
    )
)

Real-life case: Use it when a disconnected selector needs to filter a model table without creating a physical relationship.

A bridge table is usually my preferred solution when the relationship is genuinely many-to-many, but depending on the scenario other approaches include: a composite key if the relationship is only unique when multiple columns are combined; USERELATIONSHIP() when multiple possible relationships exist but only one needs activating for a given calculation; redesigning the model or changing the grain so a clean one-to-many relationship becomes possible; or DAX techniques such as TREATAS() for specific calculation scenarios.

I wouldn't use these as random replacements for a bridge table — USERELATIONSHIP() solves an inactive-relationship scenario, while a bridge solves a genuine many-to-many relationship.

OLTP/normalized schemas are optimized for transactional integrity — lots of joins, third normal form, minimal redundancy. That’s the wrong shape for analytics. Star schema denormalizes into a central fact table surrounded by dimension tables, which gives VertiPaq fewer, simpler join paths to resolve, so DAX queries are faster and filter propagation is predictable — one hop from dimension to fact instead of chaining through multiple normalized tables. It’s also easier for business users to understand: a Date, Product, and DC dimension around a Shipments fact table maps directly to how they think about the business, versus an ERD with 15 linked tables.

Both/bidirectional lets filters flow both ways, so filtering the fact table can also filter the dimension. I use bidirectional sparingly — mainly for many-to-many bridge tables — because it can create ambiguous filter paths and hurt performance. In my model I kept dimension-to-fact relationships single-direction and only turned on bidirectional filtering on the one bridge table I needed for a many-to-many product-to-region mapping.

Yes — Power BI allows multiple relationships between two tables, but only one can be active at a time; the rest are inactive. A common case is a fact table with both an Order Date and a Ship Date, both relating to the same Date dimension. The Order Date relationship is active by default; to use Ship Date in a calculation I activate it explicitly with USERELATIONSHIP() inside a CALCULATE(), rather than making it the default active path.

I check which side has unique values on the join key. If the dimension table has one row per key (e.g., one row per DC), the relationship is one-to-many from dimension to fact. I verify this with a quick Power Query or SQL profiling step — count distinct vs. total rows on the key column. If both sides have duplicates on the key, it’s actually many-to-many and needs a bridge table rather than a direct relationship.

The most common one is row multiplication/fan-out — if the “dimension” side isn’t actually unique on the key, joining causes duplicate fact rows, which silently inflates sums. Wrong cardinality also breaks filter propagation direction, causes ambiguous relationship errors, and can degrade performance because VertiPaq has to resolve many-to-many joins instead of a clean one-to-many hop. On the DC project this is exactly the kind of bug I check for first if a total looks doubled.

Yes — Power BI lets you build a hierarchy directly on top of existing columns in the model (for example Region to Department), even if the source Data Warehouse doesn't have that hierarchy physically defined.

Real-life case: I built a Region → Department → Cost Center hierarchy in the model itself on the SAR dashboard, even though the source SQL views didn't have a formal hierarchy table — it's just a drag-and-drop grouping of existing dimension columns in Model view.

Circular Dependency happens when relationships or calculated columns create a filter loop back to their own source, often from bidirectional relationships between multiple tables that all connect to each other.

Real-life case: I'd resolve it by setting relationships back to single-direction where possible, or breaking the loop by removing one redundant relationship so filters have exactly one path — this is exactly why I keep bidirectional filtering limited to the one bridge table that genuinely needs it, rather than turning it on wherever convenient.

Say: Native Power BI RLS is row-level, not a general-purpose column-level security mechanism; for different column visibility by user group, I would use separate semantic models/reports, object-level security where applicable, or an appropriate governed architecture.

Say: My hands-on RLS work was region/department based rather than a self-referencing org hierarchy. For a true manager-to-report-chain hierarchy, I'd use PATH()-based functions like PATHCONTAINS() to check if a logged-in manager's ID appears anywhere in an employee's reporting chain.

Query:

Manager RLS Filter =
PATHCONTAINS(
    Employee[HierarchyPath],
    USERPRINCIPALNAME()
)

Real-life case: This pattern would let a manager see their own row plus every employee below them in the org chart, without hardcoding a separate role per manager.

Say: Yes — OLS restricts visibility of specific tables or columns (not just rows) for certain roles, for example hiding a Salary column entirely from a role rather than filtering rows. OLS isn't configurable natively in Power BI Desktop; it's implemented using external tools like Tabular Editor, which is why I know it conceptually but haven't hands-on configured it since my project's security need was row-level, not object-level.

Real-life case: If a dashboard needed to hide a Salary or Margin column from a subset of viewers entirely — not just filter their rows — I'd open the model in Tabular Editor, set that column's object-level security to "None" for the relevant role, since Desktop has no UI for this.

For parent-child organizational hierarchies, the key DAX functions are PATH(), PATHITEM(), PATHLENGTH(), and PATHCONTAINS().

A typical approach is to build the employee hierarchy path using PATH(EmployeeID, ManagerID) and then check whether the logged-in user's employee ID exists within that hierarchy path. For simpler Dynamic RLS, I've used a mapping table with USERPRINCIPALNAME() to identify the logged-in user and propagate their authorized region or role through the model.

For sensitive columns such as Salary or confidential financial fields, I'd use Object-Level Security (OLS) to restrict access to the specific table or column for certain roles — e.g. HR leadership can view Salary, while HR analysts can access employee information but not the Salary column.

RLS controls which rows a user can see, while OLS controls access to specific tables or columns.

I'd avoid manually assigning individual users to multiple roles. Instead I'd use Security Groups where the access pattern is role-based, a UserAccess mapping table for Dynamic RLS, and USERPRINCIPALNAME() to identify the logged-in user — so access becomes data-driven and scalable. This is the same Dynamic RLS pattern I used on the SAR dashboard.

I’d build a mapping table — UserEmail to Region (one-to-many, since a manager might cover multiple regions) — and relate it to the Region dimension. The RLS role filter would be:

[UserRegion] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()

applied against the mapping table’s region column, which then filters the fact table through the existing star schema relationships. This is exactly the pattern I used for dynamic RLS on the allocation dashboard — one role, driven entirely by the mapping table, instead of hardcoding a separate static role per region.

Say: "REST APIs allow Power BI to retrieve data from external applications or services through HTTP requests. Typically, I would use Power Query's Web connector or Web.Contents() to call the API endpoint, pass required authentication such as an API key or OAuth token, and receive the response, usually in JSON format. Then I would transform and normalize the JSON data in Power Query and load it into the Power BI semantic model. For example, if I need real-time order data from an external e-commerce application, I can call its REST API, extract the order details, transform them, and build a Power BI dashboard. For scheduled reporting, I would configure the required refresh in Power BI Service."

Simple flow:

External Application → REST API → Power Query → Transform JSON → Power BI Semantic Model → Report/Dashboard

Key terms to remember: API endpoint → HTTP request → Authentication → JSON response → Power Query → Transformation → Refresh

Say: A composite model combines Import mode and DirectQuery mode within the same dataset, so different tables can use different storage modes based on how fresh they need to be.

Say: A hybrid table contains both Import and DirectQuery partitions within the same table — older data is cached in-memory while the most recent partition queries the source live.

Real-life case: Three years of historical sales stay in Import mode while today's transactions use a DirectQuery partition, giving fast historical queries plus real-time current-day numbers. It differs from plain incremental refresh, which only refreshes recent Import partitions on a schedule — a hybrid table adds a genuinely live partition on top.

Say: Partitioning splits a large table into smaller segments so a refresh only needs to process the partitions that actually changed, instead of reloading the whole table.

Real-life case: With Sales partitioned by month, a scheduled refresh only reprocesses the current month's partition instead of years of historical data.

Say: RangeStart and RangeEnd are parameters used to define the refresh window for incremental refresh; Power BI uses them to filter the source query and automatically generates the underlying partitions.

Query:

OrderDate >= RangeStart
AND OrderDate < RangeEnd

Real-life case: I've used this pattern to refresh only the last 30 days of orders on a nightly schedule instead of reloading the entire fact table.

Say: Dual Storage Mode is a setting on an individual table inside a Composite model — the table can behave as either Import or DirectQuery depending on which gives better performance for a given query. Real-life case: I'd set a shared dimension like Date or Region to Dual so it can join efficiently whether it's being queried alongside an Import fact table or a DirectQuery fact table in the same composite model.

Import loads a compressed copy of the data into VertiPaq’s in-memory columnar engine, so visuals query local memory — that’s why Import reports feel near-instant. DirectQuery sends a native query to the source database on every interaction, so performance depends entirely on the source system’s speed and indexing, and it’s almost always slower for complex DAX. The trade-off is freshness: Import means data is only as current as the last refresh, DirectQuery is real-time. On my project I used Import for the KPI dashboards since daily refresh was acceptable, and would only reach for DirectQuery/composite models if the business needed intraday numbers.

I set up RangeStart/RangeEnd parameters in Power Query, filter the fact table on the date column using those parameters, then configure the incremental refresh policy in the dataset settings — e.g., “refresh last 5 days, archive the rest as historical partitions.” Power BI then only reprocesses the recent partitions on each refresh instead of reloading the entire table, which is what makes multi-year fact tables refreshable in minutes instead of hours.

At that scale I wouldn’t rely purely on Import. My approach: strict star schema, incremental refresh so only recent partitions reload, aggregation tables at a coarser grain (e.g., daily/DC level) that most visuals hit instead of the full detail table, remove any unused or high-cardinality columns, and consider a composite model — Import for aggregates, DirectQuery for the rare drill-to-detail query. I’d also push heavy transformation logic upstream into SQL views rather than Power Query, so the engine isn’t doing row-by-row work on 500M rows.

First I’d check what’s actually driving size — usually it’s unnecessary columns, high-cardinality text columns, or calculated columns that could be measures instead. Then: enable incremental refresh so I’m not loading full history every time, build aggregation tables for common query patterns, remove columns not used in any visual or relationship, and if it’s still too large for the license tier, move to a Premium/Fabric capacity with a higher memory limit or switch part of the model to DirectQuery.

Say: In DirectQuery, source-side indexing and query-plan optimization can reduce scan time and improve response time because report interactions generate source queries.

Real-life case: I would inspect the generated SQL and source execution plan and work with the DBA to optimize indexes and expensive operations.

I'd first identify whether the issue is network connectivity, authentication, Gateway availability, source performance, or resource capacity.

Expired credentials cause authentication failures. Firewall or proxy changes can block communication between the Gateway and the data source or Power BI Service. An outdated Gateway can create compatibility, stability, or support issues.

So I'd keep credentials valid, ensure the required network communication is allowed, and keep the Gateway updated to a supported version.

If CPU, memory, or network resources are insufficient, refresh jobs can become slow, queue up, time out, or fail — especially if multiple datasets refresh simultaneously and overload the Gateway machine.

My first step is Performance Analyzer — it breaks down performance by visual and helps identify whether the delay is caused by DAX queries, visual rendering, or something else.

I'd identify the slowest visual, analyze its DAX, filters, interactions, data volume, and dependencies, and optimize the actual bottleneck rather than guessing.

Correct data types aren’t just cosmetic — they affect query folding (a mistyped column can silently break folding and push transformation load onto the local engine), storage size (a date stored as text takes far more space than a proper Date type), and correctness of aggregations and sorting. I always explicitly set types right after import rather than trusting auto-detect, especially for date and numeric columns coming from CSV sources.

I’d start with Query Diagnostics to see which step is expensive, and check whether folding broke — usually caused by a custom column, merge, or Power Query-native transformation placed before a filter step that would otherwise push down to the source. My fix order: reorder steps so filters happen as early as possible and folding stays intact, move heavy logic (joins, aggregations) back into a SQL view instead of Power Query, and set up incremental refresh so I’m not reprocessing the full history every run. I hit a version of this on my project with a 2-hour refresh caused by a non-folding merge — moving that merge into the source SQL view got it back under folding and cut the runtime significantly.

The same troubleshooting applies to a smaller version of this problem — say a refresh that normally takes 2 minutes suddenly taking 25. I'd compare what changed between the successful and slow runs: source database performance, data-volume increase, query execution time, recent Power Query changes, whether folding broke, Gateway health/resources, credential or network issues, concurrent refreshes, or a recent schema change — and isolate whether the delay is at the source, transformation, Gateway, or Power BI refresh stage.

Filtering at the source reduces the amount of data transferred and processed. Pre-aggregating data at the required reporting grain reduces row volume and can significantly improve refresh and query performance.

For example, instead of importing every transaction when the dashboard only needs monthly category-level trends, I can aggregate that data in SQL — this aligns with my project approach of using SQL views for reusable, heavier reporting logic before Power BI consumes the data.

I open Performance Analyzer first — it breaks down time spent per visual into DAX query time vs. visual rendering time vs. other. If one or two visuals dominate, I look at their DAX (usually a non-optimized measure, unnecessary bidirectional filter, or too many nested CALCULATEs). If it’s spread evenly across many visuals, it’s more likely a model-level issue — too many visuals on one page, high-cardinality columns, or unnecessary calculated columns bloating the model. I always isolate the bottleneck with data before touching anything.

Pro is a per-user license — good for smaller teams where everyone consuming reports also has a Pro license, but capped around a 1GB dataset size and limited large-model/dataflow features. Premium (or Premium-Per-User/Fabric capacity) is capacity-based rather than per-user, supports much larger datasets, XMLA endpoint access for external tools, dataflows, paginated reports, and — importantly — lets you share reports with users who don’t have Pro licenses. I’d recommend Premium once you’re distributing to a large read-only audience or your datasets are pushing past the Pro size limits, which is a real conversation on an enterprise retail deployment like mine.

I limit visuals per page, avoid unnecessary high-cardinality visuals like large tables with many columns, and remove redundant KPI cards that duplicate what a chart already shows. On one page of the SAR dashboard I replaced several overlapping small multiples with a single well-designed matrix, which cut both visual count and query load — Performance Analyzer showed the page's total render time drop noticeably once the redundant visuals were gone.

More broadly, unnecessary columns and tables increase model size, refresh time, and memory consumption, so I remove anything unused rather than keeping it “just in case.” I'm also selective with custom visuals specifically — they can add rendering overhead and inconsistent performance, so I only reach for one when a built-in visual genuinely can't do the job.

Common causes: a slow or broken DAX measure behind that visual, a filter/slicer creating an unusually large query, a broken or ambiguous relationship, DirectQuery source latency, or simply too much data/too many visuals on one page competing for rendering resources — I would check Performance Analyzer first to see exactly which query is slow or failing.

30-second answer: "For millions of records, I first optimize the model rather than immediately changing the storage mode. I use a star schema, remove unnecessary columns, reduce cardinality, use appropriate data types and keep the model in Import mode when possible. I ensure Power Query transformations fold back to the source. For very large historical data, I use incremental refresh. Depending on the workload, I can also use aggregations, composite models or DirectQuery."

Dataflow is the ETL layer, where we connect to sources and clean and transform data. Semantic model is the modeling and business-logic layer, where we create relationships, measures, and calculations. Multiple semantic models or reports can consume prepared data from a dataflow, while multiple reports can also connect to the same semantic model. So, simply, Dataflow prepares the data, Semantic Model organizes and calculates the data for reporting.

Real-life case: I kept versioned .pbix backups before major model changes so I could roll back quickly if a refactor broke a measure — a habit that's saved me more than once.

Say: Refresh success, key measure/totals validated against the source, visuals checked for broken filters, RLS roles confirmed, and a quick check on mobile/different screen sizes.

Real-life case: I always cross-check KPI totals against a raw SQL aggregate before publishing — it's the single fastest way to catch a modeling error before it reaches stakeholders.

Because this expands the "validated against the source" pre-publish check into the full three-layer validation process.

I validate in three layers: first, reconcile totals against the source system by comparing a raw SQL aggregate to the DAX measure for the same filter context; second, test edge cases — blank/null handling, filter context changes across visuals, totals vs. subtotals; third, a business-side pre-check — walking the SME through 2–3 known data points they can verify from memory before the dashboard formally goes live.

Say: Workspace: a container for content and collaboration. Semantic Model (Dataset): the data + model + measures. Report: the multi-page visual layer built on a semantic model. Dashboard: a single-page pinboard of tiles pulled from one or more reports. App: a packaged, read-only distribution of workspace content to end users.

Real-life case: I built one shared semantic model reused across three different reports, then packaged them together into a single App for distribution to the business.

Say: Copilot is a generative AI assistant built into Power BI that can draft DAX measures from natural language, summarize report visuals, suggest report pages, and answer plain-English questions about the data.

Real-life case: I've used Copilot to draft a starting point for a complex variance calculation, then reviewed and refined it manually — treating it as a fast first draft rather than a final answer.

Say: .pbix (report + full data model), .pbit (template — structure/queries without data), .pbids (a data-source shortcut file), and .pbip (Power BI Project — a Git-friendly format with separated, source-controllable files).

Real-life case: I shared a .pbit template of a dashboard's structure with a colleague so they could reuse the model and measures without me sharing live data.

Say: Premium allows up to 48 refreshes a day versus 8 on Pro, supports incremental refresh so only new/changed partitions reprocess, and runs on dedicated capacity (measured in v-cores/memory) rather than shared capacity.

Real-life case: I configured incremental refresh on a multi-year fact table so only the trailing 30 days refreshed daily — the full history stayed untouched, which is what made Premium's higher refresh frequency actually useful.

Say: Desktop is the Windows-only authoring tool for building models and reports. Service (app.powerbi.com) is the cloud platform for publishing, scheduling refresh, sharing, and collaboration. Mobile is for consuming reports and dashboards on the go, with mobile-optimized layouts.

Real-life case: I build in Desktop, publish and schedule refresh in Service, and design a mobile layout so store managers can check KPIs on their phones.

Deployment Pipelines — 30-second answer: "Deployment Pipelines provide a structured Dev-Test-Production deployment process in Power BI/Fabric. Instead of manually publishing reports between environments, I can deploy content from Development to Test and then Production. This improves governance and reduces deployment errors."

PBIP: "PBIP, or Power BI Project format, stores the Power BI project as files instead of keeping everything inside a single PBIX file. This makes it much easier to work with source control."

Git: "Git provides version control so developers can track changes, collaborate, review modifications and roll back when required."

Enterprise flow:

Developer → PBIP → Git → Development → Deployment Pipeline → Test → UAT → Production

Real-life case: "If three developers are working on an enterprise retail semantic model, PBIP and Git allow us to track changes, while Deployment Pipelines allow controlled promotion from Dev to Test to Production."

Say: I aggregate order value by customer, rank or sort the totals, and return the top three; I clarify whether ties should be included.

Query:

SELECT TOP 3
       CustomerID,
       SUM(OrderValue) AS TotalOrderValue
FROM Orders
GROUP BY CustomerID
ORDER BY TotalOrderValue DESC;

Real-life case: Identify the highest-value customers for management reporting or targeted retention.
