Say: If the result must dynamically respond to filters and aggregate data, I use a measure; if it is a stable row-level attribute needed for grouping or filtering, I consider a calculated column.

Real-life case: Total Revenue = measure; Product Risk Category = column.

Say: I use SUMX() when I need to calculate an expression row by row before aggregating it.

Query:

Revenue =
SUMX(
    Sales,
    Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]
)

Real-life case: Calculate revenue when the source does not already contain a Revenue column.

Say: I calculate current sales, previous-year sales using the Date table, then divide the variance by previous-year sales.

Query:

Sales LY =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])
)

YoY Growth % =
DIVIDE(
    [Total Sales] - [Sales LY],
    [Sales LY]
)

Real-life case: Compare current retail sales with the same period last year.

Say: I first identify the true business grain and, where appropriate, create a bridge table rather than forcing a direct many-to-many relationship.

Real-life case: Use a CustomerSegment bridge when customers can belong to multiple segments.

Say: I prefer a bridge table with unique keys on the bridge side and one-to-many relationships from the bridge to the participating tables.

Real-life case: A Customer can belong to multiple Segments, so a CustomerSegment bridge can model the relationship cleanly.

Say: I create a UserAccess mapping table, match the logged-in identity using USERPRINCIPALNAME(), and propagate the authorized key through the model.

Query:

UserAccess[UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()

Real-life case: One role can dynamically secure different regions for different managers.

Say: I choose Import when the data can be refreshed within the business requirement and interactive performance is the priority.

Real-life case: A retail dashboard with scheduled refresh and manageable model size is a strong Import candidate.

Say: I choose DirectQuery when source freshness, source-side governance, or data volume makes full import unsuitable and the source can handle interactive queries.

Real-life case: Use it for frequently changing operational data when the source is optimized for reporting queries.

Say: I choose Live Connection when an existing governed semantic or analytical model is the organization's source of truth.

Real-life case: Reuse centrally defined measures and dimensions rather than rebuilding them in every report.

Say: I push filters and required-column selection to the source, preserve foldable steps, and verify that Power Query is actually folding the transformations.

Say: I filter and select required columns early, preserve foldable steps, avoid unnecessary custom transformations before source-side filtering, and verify folding during development.

Real-life case: For a large SQL fact table, I push date and business filters to SQL Server before loading the model.

Say: I partition a large time-based fact table and refresh only the recent window while retaining historical partitions.

Real-life case: Keep years of sales history but process only the latest changing period.

Say: I monitor capacity pressure, optimize DAX/model size, use incremental refresh, stagger heavy refreshes, and investigate resource-heavy workloads.

Real-life case: If scheduled refresh overlaps with peak report usage, I reduce refresh workload and reschedule or optimize the heavy model.

Say: I first identify whether the bottleneck is the visual, DAX, model, DirectQuery source, gateway, or capacity, then optimize the largest contributor rather than guessing.

Real-life case: I would inspect Performance Analyzer, simplify expensive visuals/measures, reduce high-cardinality fields, optimize relationships, and check source query plans for DirectQuery.

My default preference is one shared semantic model with multiple reports — e.g. one governed dataset feeding a Finance Report, a Leadership Report, and an Operations Report. This avoids duplicate datasets and inconsistent KPI definitions.

I'd create separate datasets only if the divisions have fundamentally different security, performance, refresh, ownership, or data-model requirements.

I'd state assumptions clearly: Pune population approximately 7–8 million; assume around 20% are students or young professionals who are likely rucksack users; assume a replacement/purchase cycle of roughly one every 2 years; estimate the addressable annual demand and divide by 365; then adjust for online purchases and purchases made outside Pune.

The exact number matters less than demonstrating a logical structure, realistic assumptions, and a transparent calculation — this is a Fermi-estimation exercise.

I'd use a star-schema-style design. Dimensions: DimCustomer, DimSubscription/Plan, DimDate, DimLocation, DimProduct/Service. Fact tables: FactUsageEvents, FactBilling, FactPayments.

Relationships would be based on CustomerKey, SubscriptionKey, DateKey, and other surrogate keys — one customer can have multiple subscriptions, and each subscription can generate many usage events and billing records.

FactOrders
  OrderID, UserKey, OrderDateKey, ShipmentDateKey, OrderAmount

I'd connect a single DimDate twice: an active relationship OrderDateKey → DateKey, and an inactive relationship ShipmentDateKey → DateKey. For shipment-based calculations I'd activate the inactive relationship:

CALCULATE(
    [Total Orders],
    USERELATIONSHIP(FactOrders[ShipmentDateKey], DimDate[DateKey])
)

This is a classic role-playing date dimension scenario — the same pattern I'd use anywhere a fact table needs two independent date perspectives.

I'd first assess the current tools, reports, users, data sources, duplicate reports, and overlapping KPIs. Then I'd define common KPI definitions, a governed semantic/data layer, data ownership, security standards, naming/documentation standards, and approved reporting tools based on use case.

I wouldn't immediately force every existing report into one tool — I'd identify where consolidation provides value and gradually reduce duplication, aiming for a single source of truth for business metrics even if multiple presentation tools temporarily coexist.

I'd evaluate it against both technical and business criteria: the business problem it solves, integration with existing architecture, security and compliance, performance and scalability, licensing and total cost, vendor support and product maturity, maintenance requirements, user adoption/learning curve, and whether the requirement can already be solved with existing tools.

If it looks promising, I'd recommend a small proof of concept before a wider rollout.

I’d check three things in order: data volume growth (did the source table suddenly get much bigger — new region onboarded, no incremental refresh in place), whether query folding broke (someone added a step that isn’t foldable), and source-side issues (gateway performance, source database load, network). I’d use Query Diagnostics to time each step and isolate exactly where the extra time is going before changing anything.

Aggregation tables at a coarser grain for the visuals that don’t need row-level detail, strict star schema with single-direction relationships, incremental refresh, removing unused/high-cardinality columns, and disabling Auto Date/Time (it silently creates a hidden date table per date column, which is expensive at scale). If none of that is enough, I’d consider a composite model — aggregated Import layer with DirectQuery only for drill-through detail.

Depends how “near real-time” is defined. If it means minutes, I’d lean DirectQuery or a composite/hybrid model — Import for historical aggregates, DirectQuery for the current day. If it means a few times a day is fine, I’d stay on Import with scheduled refresh (or Premium’s up to 48x/day refresh), since Import performs far better and DirectQuery performance depends entirely on the source system handling the query load.

Dynamic RLS: a UserEmail-to-Region mapping table related to the Region dimension, with a role filter of [Region] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() resolved through the mapping table — the same pattern I used on the DC allocation dashboard so each regional manager only sees their own DC’s numbers without me maintaining separate static roles per region.

First I’d identify the true business key that should be unique (e.g., OrderID + LineNumber), then use ROW_NUMBER() in SQL to keep only the latest version and discard the rest — or Power Query’s Remove Duplicates step if it’s happening at the ETL layer:

WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY OrderID, LineNumber
               ORDER BY LoadDate DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Sales
)
SELECT *
FROM Ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

More importantly, I’d trace why duplicates are entering in the first place — usually a retry in the source system or a fan-out from an incorrect join upstream — and fix it at the source rather than just filtering downstream every time.

That’s the classic fan-out symptom — the “dimension” table wasn’t actually unique on the join key, so each fact row matched multiple dimension rows and got duplicated in the join. Fix: profile the dimension table for duplicates on the key, dedupe it (or fix the source), and re-verify cardinality shows one-to-many, not many-to-many, before re-checking the totals.

I reconcile step by step: confirm the date range and filters match exactly between the report and the source query, check whether RLS is silently filtering the comparison user’s view, check for timezone/currency conversion differences, check for duplicate rows from a bad join (see the fan-out issue above), and compare row counts before comparing sums — if row counts match but sums don’t, it’s a calculation logic issue; if row counts don’t match, it’s a join/filter issue.

Star schema with single-direction relationships, incremental refresh so I’m not reprocessing full history, aggregation tables for common report-level queries, appropriate (smallest possible) data types to help VertiPaq compression, removing unused columns, and avoiding calculated columns on the fact table in favor of measures. I’d also check for unnecessary high-cardinality columns like transaction-level GUIDs that don’t need to be in the reporting model at all.

I’d check the refresh history error message first — most common causes are: a schema change at the source (renamed/dropped column), an expired credential or gateway token, a gateway going offline, or data volume finally exceeding a capacity/memory limit. I’d also check if a Power Query step that relied on folding stopped folding because of an upstream source change, which can silently blow up refresh time until it eventually times out and fails.

I don’t try to satisfy both silently — I get the exact definitions each stakeholder is using in writing, show them side by side with the discrepancy, and get agreement on a single source-of-truth definition, usually escalating to whoever owns the metric if they can’t agree. On my project this came up with “stockout rate” being defined differently by two teams — I documented both definitions, built both as separate measures temporarily, and let the business decide which one became the official KPI going forward, then retired the other.

Since DirectQuery pushes every visual interaction to the source, I'd check the underlying SQL query performance first — use Performance Analyzer to capture the generated SQL, check for missing indexes on the source table, reduce visual count per page, simplify DAX to avoid heavy context transitions, and consider switching high-traffic visuals to Import/aggregation tables in a composite model. A missing index is usually the biggest single win; adding it plus reducing visual complexity typically brings load time down significantly.

At that scale, a slicer filtering the full fact table directly is expensive. I'd build aggregation tables for the common slicer-driven views, reduce cardinality on the slicer's source column, and make sure relationships are single-direction so a filter change doesn't recalculate across the whole model. Most interactions then hit the smaller aggregation table instead of the full 80-100M row fact table, which is where the real speedup comes from.

I start with the relationship setup itself: cardinality (one-to-many vs many-to-many), filter direction (single vs bidirectional), whether the relationship is active or inactive, and whether the join key's data types actually match — including hidden whitespace or case differences. A common root cause is a join key that silently changed data type (text vs number) after a source change, which breaks the relationship without any visible error.

NULLs in a join key silently drop rows or create an "unknown" blank member in the model. I clean or replace NULLs at the Power Query stage — a default value or an explicit "Unknown" placeholder row in the dimension — and use COALESCE()/ISBLANK() checks in DAX for aggregation-level handling. This keeps "Unknown" categories visible and traceable in the report instead of rows silently disappearing from totals.

Say: "I clarify the objective, users, KPI definitions, scope, and acceptance criteria, document assumptions, and confirm the requirement before building."

Real-life case: If a stakeholder changes the definition of Stockout Rate, I confirm the business definition and impact on existing measures before changing the dashboard.

Because this gives the full real-project requirements process this question asks about, grounded in the SAR project.

I start by understanding the business objective, not the visuals — what decision this report needs to support, and for whom. In my Global Direct SAR project, that meant sitting with Finance leadership and stakeholders to understand what they needed to track — company-wide spend, Budget vs. Actual vs. Prior Year comparisons, and which regions/departments/cost centers should be visible to which users. I ask about the required KPIs, filters, business rules, data sources, expected output, target users, and refresh frequency, and I document all of this clearly rather than jumping straight into development. If a requirement is ambiguous — like how a KPI should be calculated, or what "Actual" means in a given context — I ask focused questions and confirm the exact business logic with the stakeholder before building anything.

Say: "I prioritize by business impact, deadline, dependency, and effort, communicate trade-offs, and deliver the highest-value item first."

Real-life case: A regulatory or executive KPI issue takes priority over a cosmetic dashboard enhancement.

Say: "I focus on evidence rather than opinion, reproduce the issue, compare query plans/data results, discuss the trade-offs, and agree on the solution based on the business requirement."

Real-life case: If a DirectQuery report is slow, I collaborate with the DBA using the generated query and execution plan instead of blaming the source.

Say: "I follow Microsoft documentation and release updates, test relevant features in a controlled environment, and adopt them only when they solve a real business or technical problem."

Real-life case: Before introducing a new Fabric/Power BI capability into production, I validate performance, governance, licensing, and compatibility.

Say: First step: map every visual on the mock-up back to its required data fields and calculations, and confirm the data actually exists at the needed grain before building anything. Then: build the data model, core DAX measures, and one representative page first for stakeholder sign-off before finishing the rest.

Real-life case: Time estimate depends on complexity, but a single well-defined dashboard page with an existing clean data source typically takes about a week including validation, versus several weeks for a multi-page dashboard with new fiscal/security logic like the SAR project.

I break the requirement into major activities: requirement gathering, data understanding, SQL/data preparation, data modeling, DAX and KPI development, report development, testing/validation, UAT, and deployment.

I estimate effort based on complexity, dependencies, and available resources, and include a reasonable buffer for risks such as data-quality issues, changing requirements, or stakeholder feedback. I communicate the estimate along with assumptions, and if a dependency changes, I inform stakeholders early rather than waiting until the deadline.

I'd first assess the additional scope and its impact on development, testing, and dependencies, then communicate early: "The original estimate covered A, B, and C. The new requirement adds D and E, so the revised effort is X additional days."

I'd also discuss prioritization — whether some items can move to a later sprint or whether the timeline needs to be revised. The important thing is to communicate before the deadline is at risk.

I'd first assess which work items are affected and whether they're critical to the sprint goal, then inform the Scrum Lead/manager, reprioritize work, redistribute tasks based on team capacity, identify dependencies and blockers, and communicate any delivery risk early.

If the work can't realistically be completed without affecting quality, I'd recommend moving the lower-priority item to the next sprint rather than making unrealistic commitments.

Measure Dynamic calculation evaluated in filter context

Calculated Column Row-level value calculated during refresh and stored

SUM() Aggregates an existing column

Row Context Current-row evaluation

Filter Context Filters affecting a calculation

CALCULATE() Modifies filter context

Context Transition Converts row context into filter context

ALL() Removes filters

ALLSELECTED() Preserves broader user selections for visual totals

KEEPFILTERS() Intersects a new filter with the existing filter

SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR() Previous-year equivalent period

DATEADD() Shifts date context

TOTALYTD() Year-to-date calculation

RELATED() Retrieves one related value

RELATEDTABLE() Returns related rows

TREATAS() Applies one table's values as filters to another

Power Query Data ingestion and transformation

M Power Query transformation language

Merge Adds related columns

Query Folding Pushes supported transformations to source

Fact Business events/measures

Cardinality Relationship row-count pattern

CROSSFILTER() Temporarily changes relationship filtering

RLS Restricts rows by user/role

Technical Topics

SQL Hands-on

Click a topic to expand it and see the related practice questions.

Say:

“I'll use a LEFT JOIN and filter unmatched orders using IS NULL.”

SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
    ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
WHERE o.CustomerID IS NULL;

Say:

“I'll use a LEFT JOIN and find records where Table B has no match.”

SELECT a.*
FROM TableA a
LEFT JOIN TableB b
    ON a.ID = b.ID
WHERE b.ID IS NULL;

Say:

“I'll use a self-join because employees and managers are in the same table.”

SELECT e.EmployeeName, e.Salary,
       m.EmployeeName AS ManagerName,
       m.Salary AS ManagerSalary
FROM Employees e
JOIN Employees m
    ON e.ManagerID = m.EmployeeID
WHERE e.Salary > m.Salary;
SELECT
    e.EmployeeName,
    m.EmployeeName AS ManagerName,
    mm.EmployeeName AS ManagersManager
FROM Employee e
LEFT JOIN Employee m ON e.ManagerID = m.EmployeeID
LEFT JOIN Employee mm ON m.ManagerID = mm.EmployeeID;

Since employees and managers are stored in the same table, I use a self join twice: first to find the employee's manager, then again to find that manager's manager.

Say:

“I'll group by the columns that define a duplicate and filter counts greater than one.”

SELECT Name, COUNT(*) AS DuplicateCount
FROM Employees
GROUP BY Name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Say:

“I'll multiply quantity by unit price and aggregate the result by product.”

SELECT ProductID,
       SUM(Quantity * UnitPrice) AS TotalRevenue
FROM Sales
GROUP BY ProductID;

Say:

“Because I'm filtering an aggregate, I'll use HAVING instead of WHERE.”

SELECT DepartmentID,
       SUM(Salary) AS TotalSalary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY DepartmentID
HAVING SUM(Salary) > 100000;

Say:

“I'll group sales by region and calculate the average.”

SELECT Region,
       AVG(SalesAmount) AS AvgSales
FROM Sales
GROUP BY Region;

Say:

“I'll aggregate revenue by region, sort it descending and return the top three.”

SELECT TOP 3 Region,
       SUM(Revenue) AS TotalRevenue
FROM Sales
GROUP BY Region
ORDER BY TotalRevenue DESC;
SELECT Country
FROM Customers
GROUP BY Country;

GROUP BY Country creates one group per unique country, so it can be used to return unique values without using DISTINCT.

Say:

“I'll first find the maximum salary and then find the maximum salary below it.”

SELECT MAX(Salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employees
WHERE Salary < (
    SELECT MAX(Salary)
    FROM Employees
);

Say:

“I'll calculate the average salary in a subquery and compare each employee against it.”

SELECT EmployeeID, EmployeeName, Salary
FROM Employees
WHERE Salary > (
    SELECT AVG(Salary)
    FROM Employees
);

Say:

“I'll sort employees by salary in descending order and return the top three.”

SELECT TOP 3 EmployeeID, EmployeeName, Salary
FROM Employees
ORDER BY Salary DESC;

Say:

“I'll use NOT EXISTS to find products with no matching sales record.”

SELECT p.ProductID, p.ProductName
FROM Products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM Sales s
    WHERE s.ProductID = p.ProductID
);
WITH RankedSalary AS (
    SELECT EmployeeID, EmployeeName, Salary,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS SalaryRank
    FROM Employee
)
SELECT * FROM RankedSalary WHERE SalaryRank = 10;

I use DENSE_RANK() because if multiple employees share a salary, they get the same rank, so I still land on the 10th highest distinct salary. An alternative is OFFSET/FETCH:

SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM Employee
ORDER BY Salary DESC
OFFSET 9 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROW ONLY;

For interview purposes, DENSE_RANK() is usually the clearer approach for Nth highest distinct values.

Say:

“I'll use ROW_NUMBER() inside a CTE to identify duplicates and then delete rows having a row number greater than one.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY Name
               ORDER BY EmployeeID
           ) AS rn
    FROM Employees
)
DELETE FROM CTE
WHERE rn > 1;

Say:

“I'll use a CTE to break the complex logic into readable steps.”

WITH SalesSummary AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           SUM(Amount) AS TotalSales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT CustomerID, TotalSales
FROM SalesSummary
WHERE TotalSales > 10000;

Say:

“I'll rank salaries using DENSE_RANK() and filter for the required rank.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM Employees
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rnk = 3;

Say:

“I'll use SUM() as a window function ordered by the sale date.”

SELECT SaleDate,
       SalesAmount,
       SUM(SalesAmount) OVER (
           ORDER BY SaleDate
       ) AS RunningTotal
FROM Sales;

Say:

“I'll rank transactions separately for each user using DENSE_RANK().”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY UserID
               ORDER BY Amount DESC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM Transactions
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rnk = 2;

Say:

“I'll use LAG() to compare the current month's sales with the previous month.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT Month,
           Sales,
           LAG(Sales) OVER (ORDER BY Month) AS PreviousSales
    FROM MonthlySales
)
SELECT *,
       Sales - PreviousSales AS SalesIncrease
FROM CTE
WHERE Sales > PreviousSales;

Say:

“I'll divide product revenue by the overall revenue using a window function.”

SELECT ProductID,
       SUM(Revenue) AS ProductRevenue,
       SUM(Revenue) * 100.0 /
       SUM(SUM(Revenue)) OVER () AS RevenuePercentage
FROM Sales
GROUP BY ProductID;

Say:

“I'll use ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by customer and order by date descending.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY CustomerID
               ORDER BY OrderDate DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Orders
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rn = 2;

Say:

“ROW_NUMBER() gives every row a unique number. RANK() gives the same rank to ties but skips ranks. DENSE_RANK() gives the same rank to ties without skipping ranks.”

SELECT EmployeeName,
       Salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS RankNum,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS DenseRankNum
FROM Employees;

Say:

“I'll partition the ranking by department.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY DepartmentID
               ORDER BY Salary DESC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM Employees
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rnk = 2;

Say:

"LAG() looks at the previous row's value, LEAD() looks at the next row's value, both within a partition/order — useful for period-over-period comparisons without a self-join."

SELECT
    SKU,
    SaleDate,
    Inventory,
    LAG(Inventory) OVER (PARTITION BY SKU ORDER BY SaleDate) AS PrevInventory,
    LEAD(Inventory) OVER (PARTITION BY SKU ORDER BY SaleDate) AS NextInventory
FROM Inventory;

Real-life case: Used LAG(Inventory) OVER (PARTITION BY SKU ORDER BY Date) to flag sudden inventory drops that could indicate a data or allocation error on the SAR project.

---

Say:

“I'll rank products within each category and select rank one.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT ProductID, Category,
           SUM(SalesAmount) AS TotalSales,
           RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY Category
               ORDER BY SUM(SalesAmount) DESC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY ProductID, Category
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rnk = 1;

Say:

“I'll aggregate revenue by product and return the top three.”

SELECT TOP 3 ProductID,
       SUM(Revenue) AS TotalRevenue
FROM Sales
GROUP BY ProductID
ORDER BY TotalRevenue DESC;

Say:

“I'll first calculate product-level sales, select the top five and divide their sales by total sales.”

WITH ProductSales AS (
    SELECT TOP 5 ProductID,
           SUM(SalesAmount) AS Sales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY ProductID
    ORDER BY Sales DESC
)
SELECT SUM(Sales) * 100.0 /
       (SELECT SUM(SalesAmount) FROM Sales) AS Top5Percentage
FROM ProductSales;

Say:

“I'll group by the duplicate-defining columns and check where the count is greater than one.”

SELECT Name, COUNT(*) AS Cnt
FROM Employees
GROUP BY Name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Say:

“I'll assign row numbers within each duplicate group and delete rows after the first.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY Name
               ORDER BY EmployeeID
           ) AS rn
    FROM Employees
)
DELETE FROM CTE
WHERE rn > 1;

Say:

“I'll use MIN() for the first purchase and MAX() for the last purchase.”

SELECT CustomerID,
       MIN(PurchaseDate) AS FirstPurchase,
       MAX(PurchaseDate) AS LastPurchase
FROM Orders
GROUP BY CustomerID;

Say:

“I'll find customers whose latest purchase is older than six months or who have never purchased.”

SELECT CustomerID
FROM Orders
GROUP BY CustomerID
HAVING MAX(OrderDate) < DATEADD(MONTH, -6, GETDATE());

Say:

“I'll aggregate monthly spending and use LAG() to compare it with the previous month.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS Month,
           SUM(Amount) AS Sales
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID,
             DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1)
),
CompareSales AS (
    SELECT *,
           LAG(Sales) OVER (
               PARTITION BY CustomerID
               ORDER BY Month
           ) AS PreviousSales
    FROM CTE
)
SELECT *
FROM CompareSales
WHERE Sales > PreviousSales;

Say:

“I'll filter the required date range and then use MIN() and MAX().”

SELECT CustomerID,
       MIN(TransactionDate) AS FirstTransaction,
       MAX(TransactionDate) AS LastTransaction
FROM Transactions
WHERE TransactionDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-06-30'
GROUP BY CustomerID;

Say:

“I'll find the first and last order dates and use DATEDIFF().”

SELECT CustomerID,
       DATEDIFF(
           DAY,
           MIN(OrderDate),
           MAX(OrderDate)
       ) AS DaysBetweenOrders
FROM Orders
GROUP BY CustomerID;

Say:

“I'll compare each purchase month with the previous purchase month using LAG().”

WITH Months AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT
           CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS Month
    FROM Orders
),
CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           LAG(Month) OVER (
               PARTITION BY CustomerID
               ORDER BY Month
           ) AS PreviousMonth
    FROM Months
)
SELECT DISTINCT CustomerID
FROM CTE
WHERE DATEDIFF(MONTH, PreviousMonth, Month) = 1;

Say:

“I'll extract the year and month from the date and aggregate sales.”

SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS Year,
       MONTH(OrderDate) AS Month,
       SUM(Amount) AS TotalSales
FROM Orders
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate),
         MONTH(OrderDate)
ORDER BY Year, Month;

Say:

“I'll find the customer's latest order and check whether it is older than six months.”

SELECT CustomerID,
       MAX(OrderDate) AS LastOrderDate
FROM Orders
GROUP BY CustomerID
HAVING MAX(OrderDate) < DATEADD(MONTH, -6, GETDATE());

Say:

“I'll use CASE WHEN to create conditional categories.”

SELECT EmployeeID,
       Salary,
       CASE
           WHEN Salary < 50000 THEN 'Low'
           WHEN Salary < 100000 THEN 'Medium'
           ELSE 'High'
       END AS SalaryCategory
FROM Employees;

Say:

“I'll use conditional aggregation with CASE WHEN.”

SELECT CustomerID,
       SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Jan' THEN Sales ELSE 0 END) AS JanSales,
       SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Feb' THEN Sales ELSE 0 END) AS FebSales,
       SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Mar' THEN Sales ELSE 0 END) AS MarSales
FROM Sales
GROUP BY CustomerID;

Say:

“Aggregate functions cannot be used directly in WHERE; I'll use HAVING after the GROUP BY.”

❌ Incorrect:

SELECT DepartmentID, SUM(Salary)
FROM Employees
WHERE SUM(Salary) > 100000
GROUP BY DepartmentID;

✅ Correct:

SELECT DepartmentID,
       SUM(Salary) AS TotalSalary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY DepartmentID
HAVING SUM(Salary) > 100000;

Say:

“I'll use LAG() to compare the current value with the previous two rows.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT ID,
           Value,
           LAG(Value, 1) OVER (ORDER BY ID) AS Prev1,
           LAG(Value, 2) OVER (ORDER BY ID) AS Prev2
    FROM DataTable
)
SELECT ID, Value
FROM CTE
WHERE Value = Prev1
  AND Value = Prev2;

Say:

“I'll compare each invoice number with the previous invoice number using LAG() and identify gaps greater than one.”

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT InvoiceNo,
           LAG(InvoiceNo) OVER (
               ORDER BY InvoiceNo
           ) AS PreviousInvoice
    FROM Invoices
)
SELECT PreviousInvoice + 1 AS MissingFrom,
       InvoiceNo - 1 AS MissingTo
FROM CTE
WHERE InvoiceNo - PreviousInvoice > 1;
WITH MonthlyData AS (
    SELECT ProductID, SalesMonth, SUM(UnitsSold) AS UnitsSold
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY ProductID, SalesMonth
),
Trend AS (
    SELECT
        ProductID, SalesMonth, UnitsSold,
        LAG(UnitsSold, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductID ORDER BY SalesMonth) AS Prev1,
        LAG(UnitsSold, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductID ORDER BY SalesMonth) AS Prev2,
        LAG(SalesMonth, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductID ORDER BY SalesMonth) AS PrevMonth2
    FROM MonthlyData
)
SELECT ProductID
FROM Trend
WHERE UnitsSold > Prev1
  AND Prev1 > Prev2
  AND DATEDIFF(MONTH, PrevMonth2, SalesMonth) = 2;

I first aggregate to the Product-Month level, then use LAG() to compare the current month with the previous two months, and finally ensure the sales are increasing and the months are consecutive.

SQL’s logical processing order is FROM → JOIN/ON → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY — even though we type SELECT first. So for:

SELECT p.ProductName, SUM(s.Revenue)
FROM Sales s
LEFT JOIN Product p ON s.ProductID = p.ProductID
WHERE s.OrderDate >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY p.ProductName;

the engine first joins Sales to Product row by row matching ProductID, then applies the date filter, then groups and aggregates, and only at the end resolves the SELECT list. I’d walk through 3–4 sample rows on a whiteboard to show exactly which rows survive each stage.

Senior Analyst Interview Round

SQL TOPICS MOST ASKED

Interview-ready SQL topics with questions, “Say” answers, queries, and real-life cases.

SQL commands are categorized based on their purpose.

DDL (Data Definition Language) is used to define and manage database objects such as tables and schemas (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE).

DML (Data Manipulation Language) is used to insert, update, delete, or merge data within tables (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE).

DQL (Data Query Language) is used to retrieve data from the database using the SELECT statement.

DCL (Data Control Language) is used to manage user permissions and access control (GRANT, REVOKE).

Structured Data is organized in a predefined format, typically rows and columns, and is stored in relational databases such as SQL Server, MySQL, or Oracle.

Unstructured Data does not follow a fixed schema and includes files such as images, videos, PDFs, emails, audio files, and social media content. It is commonly stored in data lakes, cloud storage, or NoSQL databases.

SQL uses several types of keys to uniquely identify records and establish relationships between tables.

Key TypeDescription
Primary KeyA column (or combination of columns) that uniquely identifies each record in a table. It cannot contain NULL values and must be unique. Example: EmployeeID in an Employees table.
Foreign KeyA column that creates a relationship between two tables by referencing the Primary Key of another table. It maintains referential integrity. Example: DepartmentID in Employees referencing the Departments table.
Candidate KeyAny column or set of columns that can uniquely identify a record. A table can have multiple candidate keys, but only one is chosen as the Primary Key. Example: EmployeeID and EmailID both uniquely identify employees.
Super KeyAny combination of columns that uniquely identifies a record. It may contain extra unnecessary columns. Example: (EmployeeID, Name) is a super key if EmployeeID alone is unique.
Alternate KeyCandidate keys that are not selected as the Primary Key. Example: if EmployeeID is the Primary Key, then EmailID becomes an Alternate Key.
Composite KeyA key made up of two or more columns that together uniquely identify a record. Example: (OrderID, ProductID) in an OrderDetails table.
Unique KeyEnsures all values in a column are unique. Unlike a Primary Key, it can allow one NULL value (SQL Server). A table can have multiple Unique Keys.
Secondary KeyA non-unique column used mainly for searching and retrieving data efficiently. Example: City column in a Customer table — multiple customers can belong to the same city.
Surrogate KeyA system-generated unique identifier with no business meaning. Commonly implemented using IDENTITY or auto-increment columns. Example: CustomerID = 1001, 1002, 1003.

CHAR is a fixed-length data type. It always reserves the specified amount of storage and pads unused space with blanks. It is suitable for storing fixed-length values such as country codes.

VARCHAR is a variable-length data type that stores only the actual data entered, making it more storage-efficient for values with varying lengths such as names and addresses.

VARCHAR stores non-Unicode characters and typically uses 1 byte per character, making it suitable for English-only data.

NVARCHAR stores Unicode characters and uses 2 bytes per character, allowing it to support multiple languages and special characters.

CHAR is a fixed-length, non-Unicode data type used for storing fixed-size character data.

NCHAR is also fixed-length but stores Unicode characters, making it suitable for multilingual applications where support for multiple languages is required.

Imagine you're counting people in an office:

  • COUNT(*) → Count everyone in the office.
  • COUNT(1) → Count everyone (same as above).
  • COUNT(Name) → Count only people wearing an ID card (non-NULL names).
  • COUNT('a') / COUNT(-1) → Give every person a token, then count the tokens. Since everyone gets one, the count equals the number of rows.

Say: ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique sequential number to every row within the specified window, even when values are tied.

Query:

SELECT *,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY transaction_date DESC, transaction_id DESC
       ) AS rn
FROM Transactions;

Real-life case: Use it to select the latest transaction for each customer or remove duplicate customer records.

Say: RANK() gives tied rows the same rank and skips the next rank after a tie.

Query:

SELECT employee_name, salary,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
FROM Employees;

Real-life case: Rank employees or products by performance where tied values should share the same position.

Say: DENSE_RANK() gives tied rows the same rank but does not leave gaps.

Query:

SELECT employee_name, salary,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
FROM Employees;

Real-life case: Find the Nth highest distinct salary or rank products within a category.

Say: ROW_NUMBER = unique numbers; RANK = ties with gaps; DENSE_RANK = ties without gaps.

Real-life case: Use ROW_NUMBER for deduplication, RANK for competition-style ranking, and DENSE_RANK for Nth distinct values.

Related Questions

Because this is the direct hands-on version of explaining all three ranking functions with sample data.

Say:

"ROW_NUMBER() gives every row a unique number. RANK() gives the same rank to ties but skips ranks. DENSE_RANK() gives the same rank to ties without skipping ranks."

SELECT EmployeeName,
       Salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS RankNum,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS DenseRankNum
FROM Employees;

Say: For the second-highest distinct salary, I would generally use DENSE_RANK() and filter for rank 2.

Query:

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT salary,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
    FROM Employees
)
SELECT salary
FROM ranked
WHERE drnk = 2;

Alternative:

SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM Employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employees);

Real-life case: Find the second-best-selling product or second-highest employee salary while handling duplicate values correctly.

Related Questions

Because this is the direct hands-on version of the same problem, using a simpler MAX()-based approach.

Say:

"I'll first find the maximum salary and then find the maximum salary below it."

SELECT MAX(Salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employees
WHERE Salary < (
    SELECT MAX(Salary)
    FROM Employees
);

Say: I use DENSE_RANK() for the Nth highest distinct value because duplicate values receive the same rank.

Query:

DECLARE @N INT = 3;

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT salary,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM Employees
)
SELECT salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = @N;

Real-life case: Find the Nth-highest distinct salary, product, or customer metric by changing @N.

Related Questions

Because this is the direct hands-on version of the same DENSE_RANK() Nth-highest pattern.

Say:

"I'll rank salaries using DENSE_RANK() and filter for the required rank."

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM Employees
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rnk = 3;

Say: I aggregate by customer, sum order value, sort descending, and return the top three.

Query:

SELECT TOP 3
       customer_id,
       SUM(order_value) AS total_order_value
FROM Orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY total_order_value DESC;

Real-life case: Identify the top three customers contributing the highest sales.

Related Questions

Because this is the same GROUP BY + TOP N aggregation pattern applied to products instead of customers.

Say:

"I'll aggregate revenue by product and return the top three."

SELECT TOP 3 ProductID,
       SUM(Revenue) AS TotalRevenue
FROM Sales
GROUP BY ProductID
ORDER BY TotalRevenue DESC;

Say: I first aggregate customer sales, then use DENSE_RANK() when I want to include ties at the third rank; if I need exactly three customers, I use TOP 3 or ROW_NUMBER().

Query:

WITH customer_sales AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           SUM(order_value) AS total_order_value
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_order_value DESC) AS sales_rank
    FROM customer_sales
)
SELECT customer_id, total_order_value
FROM ranked
WHERE sales_rank <= 3;

Real-life case: Include all customers tied within the top three sales ranks; this can return more than three customers when ties occur.

Related Questions

Because this uses the same aggregate-then-window-function ranking pattern, just per-category instead of per-overall-total.

Say:

"I'll rank products within each category and select rank one."

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT ProductID, Category,
           SUM(SalesAmount) AS TotalSales,
           RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY Category
               ORDER BY SUM(SalesAmount) DESC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY ProductID, Category
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rnk = 1;

Say: Window functions calculate across related rows without collapsing the individual rows.

Query:

SELECT employee_name, department, salary,
       SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS department_total
FROM Employees;

Real-life case: Show each product's sales alongside the total sales of its category.

Say: OVER() defines the set of rows used by a window function and can contain PARTITION BY and ORDER BY.

Query:

SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)

Real-life case: Calculate a running sales total while keeping each daily sales row.

Say: PARTITION BY divides rows into logical groups so the window calculation runs independently for each group.

Query:

SUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)

Real-life case: Calculate each customer's total sales while retaining every transaction.

Say: It defines the sequence of rows used by ranking, running totals, LAG() and LEAD().

Query:

SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)

Real-life case: Calculate sales cumulatively from the earliest date to the latest.

Say: I use SUM() OVER(ORDER BY date) to accumulate values from the first row through the current row.

Query:

WITH DailySales AS (
    SELECT order_date,
           SUM(sales) AS daily_sales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY order_date
)
SELECT order_date,
       daily_sales,
       SUM(daily_sales) OVER (
           ORDER BY order_date
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS cumulative_sales
FROM DailySales;

Real-life case: Track cumulative monthly retail revenue through the year.

Related Questions

Because this is the direct hands-on version of the same running-total window function.

Say:

"I'll use SUM() as a window function ordered by the sale date."

SELECT SaleDate,
       SalesAmount,
       SUM(SalesAmount) OVER (
           ORDER BY SaleDate
       ) AS RunningTotal
FROM Sales;

Say: A running sum accumulates from the beginning, while a rolling sum uses a fixed moving window; ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means three rows, not necessarily three months.

Query:

\-- Running total
SUM(sales) OVER (
    ORDER BY order_date
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
)

\-- Rolling 3 rows
SUM(sales) OVER (
    ORDER BY order_date
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
)

Real-life case: Running revenue shows year-to-date performance; rolling sales can show the latest moving trend.

Say: LAG() gets a previous row's value, while LEAD() gets a following row's value.

Query:

SELECT order_date, sales,
       LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS previous_sales,
       LEAD(sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS next_sales
FROM Sales;

Real-life case: Compare current-month sales with previous-month sales.

Related Questions

Because this is the same LAG()/LEAD() pattern applied to a real project scenario — flagging sudden inventory drops.

Say:

"LAG() looks at the previous row's value, LEAD() looks at the next row's value, both within a partition/order — useful for period-over-period comparisons without a self-join."

SELECT
    SKU,
    SaleDate,
    Inventory,
    LAG(Inventory) OVER (PARTITION BY SKU ORDER BY SaleDate) AS PrevInventory,
    LEAD(Inventory) OVER (PARTITION BY SKU ORDER BY SaleDate) AS NextInventory
FROM Inventory;

Real-life case: Used LAG(Inventory) OVER (PARTITION BY SKU ORDER BY Date) to flag sudden inventory drops that could indicate a data or allocation error on the SAR project.

Because this is the direct hands-on version of comparing current-month sales with the previous month using LAG().

Say:

"I'll use LAG() to compare the current month's sales with the previous month."

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT Month,
           Sales,
           LAG(Sales) OVER (ORDER BY Month) AS PreviousSales
    FROM MonthlySales
)
SELECT *,
       Sales - PreviousSales AS SalesIncrease
FROM CTE
WHERE Sales > PreviousSales;

Say: GROUP BY collapses rows into one row per group, while PARTITION BY groups rows for a window calculation and keeps the original rows.

Real-life case: Use GROUP BY for a category-level sales table; use PARTITION BY when each product row also needs its category total.

Say: I partition by the duplicate-defining columns, assign ROW_NUMBER(), and treat rows with rn > 1 as duplicates.

Query:

WITH RankedCustomers AS (
    SELECT customer_id, customer_name, email,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY email
               ORDER BY customer_id
           ) AS rn
    FROM Customers
)
SELECT *
FROM RankedCustomers
WHERE rn > 1;

Real-life case: Identify duplicate customer records based on email.

Related Questions

Because this is an alternate technique (GROUP BY/HAVING instead of ROW_NUMBER) for solving the same duplicate-finding problem.

Say:

"I'll group by the duplicate-defining columns and check where the count is greater than one."

SELECT Name, COUNT(*) AS Cnt
FROM Employees
GROUP BY Name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Say: I identify duplicates with ROW_NUMBER(), keep rn = 1, and delete rows where rn > 1; in production I first verify the SELECT result.

Query:

WITH RankedCustomers AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY email
               ORDER BY customer_id
           ) AS rn
    FROM Customers
)
DELETE c
FROM Customers c
INNER JOIN RankedCustomers r
    ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id
WHERE r.rn > 1;

Real-life case: Keep the first customer record and remove repeated records with the same email.

Related Questions

Because this is the direct hands-on version of the same ROW_NUMBER()-based delete-duplicates pattern.

Say:

"I'll assign row numbers within each duplicate group and delete rows after the first."

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY Name
               ORDER BY EmployeeID
           ) AS rn
    FROM Employees
)
DELETE FROM CTE
WHERE rn > 1;

Say: I'd use LAG() partitioned by product and ordered by month to compare each month's sales against the previous one, flag whether it increased, then use a window count or a CTE with conditional aggregation to check that the flag was true for the last 3 consecutive months per product.

Query:

WITH MonthlyTrend AS (
    SELECT
        ProductID,
        SalesMonth,
        MonthlySales,
        CASE WHEN MonthlySales > LAG(MonthlySales) OVER (
            PARTITION BY ProductID ORDER BY SalesMonth
        ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS IsUp
    FROM MonthlySalesSummary
)
SELECT ProductID
FROM MonthlyTrend
GROUP BY ProductID
HAVING SUM(IsUp) >= 3;

Real-life case: This pattern generalizes to any "N consecutive periods of improvement" business question, not just sales.

Related Questions

Because this uses the same LAG()-based consecutive-period detection pattern, applied to customer purchase months instead of sales trend.

Say:

"I'll compare each purchase month with the previous purchase month using LAG()."

WITH Months AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT
           CustomerID,
           DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS Month
    FROM Orders
),
CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           LAG(Month) OVER (
               PARTITION BY CustomerID
               ORDER BY Month
           ) AS PreviousMonth
    FROM Months
)
SELECT DISTINCT CustomerID
FROM CTE

Say: I've used aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, COUNT), window/ranking functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG, LEAD), scalar functions (GETDATE, ISNULL, CAST), and string functions for cleaning data extensively for reporting and validation.

Real-life case: On the SAR project, window functions handled ranking and period-over-period comparisons, while scalar and string functions handled the data-cleaning layer before it reached the reporting views.

Say: No — SUMX and AVERAGEX are DAX iterator functions, not SQL window functions. They loop row-by-row over a table expression and evaluate an expression for each row before aggregating, which is conceptually similar to a window function's per-row evaluation, but it's a DAX-specific pattern, not the SQL OVER()/PARTITION BY mechanism.

Real-life case: I'm careful not to conflate the two in an interview — DAX iterators and SQL window functions solve a similar row-by-row problem but live in completely different engines with different syntax.

Say: In DAX, COUNT counts numeric/date values in a column and ignores blanks and text, while COUNTA counts any non-blank value regardless of type, including text. In SQL, COUNT(column) skips NULLs while COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of NULLs.

Real-life case: I use COUNT(*) when I need a raw row count for validation, and COUNT(column) specifically when I need to know how many rows actually have a value in that field.

Both give the same rank to tied values — the difference is what happens after the tie. For salaries 100, 90, 90, 80: RANK() gives 1, 2, 2, 4 (a gap), while DENSE_RANK() gives 1, 2, 2, 3 (no gap).

I generally use DENSE_RANK() when I need the Nth highest distinct value.

SELECT
    EmployeeName,
    Salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS RowNum,
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS RankNum,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS DenseRankNum
FROM Employee;

For salaries 100, 90, 90, 80: ROW_NUMBER gives 1,2,3,4 (always unique), RANK gives 1,2,2,4 (ties share a rank, next rank skips), DENSE_RANK gives 1,2,2,3 (ties share a rank, no skip).

Say: INNER JOIN returns only rows with matching keys in both tables.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

Real-life case: Return only orders that have a matching customer record.

Say: LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table and matching rows from the right table, with NULL when there is no match.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

Real-life case: Find all customers, including customers who have never placed an order.

Related Questions

Because this is the direct hands-on version of the exact LEFT JOIN + IS NULL anti-pattern this topic explains.

Say:

"I'll use a LEFT JOIN and filter unmatched orders using IS NULL."

SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
    ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
WHERE o.CustomerID IS NULL;

Say: RIGHT JOIN returns every row from the right table plus matching rows from the left; in practice, I usually rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN by switching the table order because it is easier to read.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM Orders o
RIGHT JOIN Customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

Real-life case: Preserve every customer record while joining order information.

Say: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matching and non-matching rows from both tables.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM Customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN Orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

Real-life case: Reconcile two source systems and identify records missing from either side.

Say: CROSS JOIN creates the Cartesian product by combining every row from one table with every row from the other.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM Products
CROSS JOIN Stores;

Real-life case: Generate every possible product-store combination only when the business requirement genuinely needs it, because the result can grow very quickly.

Say: A self join joins a table to itself and is commonly used for hierarchical relationships.

Query:

SELECT e.employee_name,
       m.employee_name AS manager_name
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN Employees m
    ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;

Real-life case: Map each employee to their manager from the same employee table.

Related Questions

Because this is the direct hands-on version of a self-join solving a real employee/manager comparison problem.

Say:

"I'll use a self-join because employees and managers are in the same table."

SELECT e.EmployeeName, e.Salary,
       m.EmployeeName AS ManagerName,
       m.Salary AS ManagerSalary
FROM Employees e
JOIN Employees m
    ON e.ManagerID = m.EmployeeID
WHERE e.Salary > m.Salary;

Say: INNER = matching only; LEFT = all left; RIGHT = all right; FULL = both sides; CROSS = every combination; SELF = same table.

Real-life case: Choose the join based on whether unmatched records must be retained.

Related Questions

Because this walks through the actual execution order (FROM → JOIN/ON → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY) that determines how each join type behaves in practice.

SQL's logical processing order is FROM → JOIN/ON → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY — even though we type SELECT first.

Tables: Customers, Orders

SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL;

Interview Follow-up: Why LEFT JOIN and not INNER JOIN?

Tables: Employees

SELECT e.emp_name, e.salary, m.emp_name AS manager
FROM Employees e
JOIN Employees m
ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

Tests: Self Join concept.

Tables: Employee, Department

SELECT d.department_name,
       MAX(e.salary) AS highest_salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_name;

Follow-up: Show employee name also.

SELECT d.department_name
FROM Department d
LEFT JOIN Employee e
ON d.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE e.employee_id IS NULL;

Very common LEFT JOIN scenario.

SELECT e.*
FROM Employee e
LEFT JOIN Department d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id
WHERE d.department_id IS NULL;

Tests NULL handling.

Tables: Sales, Product

SELECT p.category,
       SUM(s.sales_amount)
FROM Sales s
JOIN Product p
ON s.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.category;

Most common business scenario.

WITH cte AS
(
SELECT p.category,
       p.product_name,
       SUM(s.sales_amount) sales,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER
       (PARTITION BY p.category
        ORDER BY SUM(s.sales_amount) DESC) rnk
FROM Sales s
JOIN Product p
ON s.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.category,p.product_name
)
SELECT *
FROM cte
WHERE rnk = 1;

Tests JOIN + Window Function.

WITH cte AS
(
SELECT c.customer_name,
       o.order_date,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER
       (PARTITION BY c.customer_id
        ORDER BY o.order_date DESC) rn
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o
ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
)
SELECT *
FROM cte
WHERE rn = 1;

Very popular in product companies.

SELECT *
FROM Employee e
LEFT JOIN Department d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id
AND d.department_name = 'IT';

vs

SELECT *
FROM Employee e
LEFT JOIN Department d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id
WHERE d.department_name = 'IT';

Expected Answer:

  • Condition in ON preserves LEFT JOIN.
  • Condition in WHERE may convert LEFT JOIN into INNER JOIN.

Interviewer gives:

Table A

id
1
1
2

Table B

id
1
1
1
2
SELECT *
FROM A
INNER JOIN B
ON A.id = B.id;

Expected answer:

  • For id=1 → 2 × 3 = 6 rows
  • For id=2 → 1 × 1 = 1 row
  • Total = 7 rows

We have two tables:

Employee — EmployeeID | EmployeeName | DepartmentID | Salary

Department — DepartmentID | DepartmentName

Interview Answer (30 seconds):

"I would first join the Employee and Department tables using DepartmentID. Then I would use the DENSE_RANK() window function and partition the data by DepartmentID while ordering salaries in descending order. This assigns rank 1 to the highest salary within each department. Finally, I would filter for rank = 1 to get the highest-paid employee from every department. I prefer DENSE_RANK() because if multiple employees have the same highest salary, all of them will be returned."

SQL Query

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT
        e.EmployeeID,
        e.EmployeeName,
        d.DepartmentName,
        e.Salary,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (
            PARTITION BY e.DepartmentID
            ORDER BY e.Salary DESC
        ) AS rnk
    FROM Employee e
    JOIN Department d
        ON e.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rnk = 1;

Follow-up Question: How would you find the 2nd highest salary in each department?

Answer: "I would use the same query and simply change WHERE rnk = 1 to WHERE rnk = 2."

WHERE rnk = 2;

A good next practice question is: "Find the top 3 highest-paid employees in each department." That's one of the most common SQL interview follow-ups after this question.

SELECT
    e.emp_id,
    e.emp_name,
    m.emp_name AS manager_name
FROM Employee e
LEFT JOIN Employee m
    ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;

Answer: Self Join because employee and manager are stored in the same table.

SELECT
    e.emp_name,
    e.salary,
    m.emp_name AS manager_name,
    m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m
    ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

Follow-up: Why self join? Because manager details are in the same table.

SELECT e.emp_name
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m
    ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id
WHERE m.emp_name = 'John';
SELECT
    m.emp_name AS manager_name,
    COUNT(*) AS team_size
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m
    ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id
GROUP BY m.emp_name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
SELECT TOP 1
    m.emp_name,
    COUNT(*) AS team_size
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m
    ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id
GROUP BY m.emp_name
ORDER BY team_size DESC;

Say: I start from the transaction table and join Customer and Product using their keys.

Query:

SELECT c.CustomerName,
       p.ProductName,
       s.SalesAmount
FROM Sales s
INNER JOIN Customer c
    ON s.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
INNER JOIN Product p
    ON s.ProductID = p.ProductID;

Real-life case: Produce a report showing customer, product and sales amount for every transaction.

Say: Duplicate join-key values on either side multiply into every matching combination, so the joined result can have far more rows than either source table.

Real-life case: If Orders has one row with ProductID P1 and Products has two rows with ProductID P1, the join returns two P1 rows instead of one — I'd fix this by deduplicating the smaller table with DISTINCT or verifying the join key is actually unique before joining.

Say: For INNER JOINs the final result set is usually the same regardless of table order, but the execution plan — and therefore performance — can differ, especially with a big size difference between tables.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM SmallTable S
JOIN LargeTable L
    ON S.ID = L.ID;

Real-life case: When joining a 100M-row table to a 1M-row table, I filter and reduce the smaller table first so the optimizer has less data to match against.

Say: In a LEFT JOIN, a condition in ON is applied before the join and still preserves all left-table rows, while the same condition in WHERE is applied after the join and silently turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.

Query:

-- Condition in ON: preserves all rows from A
SELECT *
FROM A
LEFT JOIN B ON A.ID = B.ID
    AND B.Status = 'Active';

-- Condition in WHERE: behaves like an INNER JOIN
SELECT *
FROM A
LEFT JOIN B ON A.ID = B.ID
WHERE B.Status = 'Active';

Real-life case: This is one of the most commonly asked SQL interview questions — I always double-check filter placement whenever a LEFT JOIN unexpectedly drops rows.

Say: An INNER JOIN returns one row for every matching combination — so if the join key has duplicates on both sides, the result is the product of the matching duplicate counts for that key, not just 5 or 3. For example, 5 matching rows on one side against 3 on the other for the same key returns 15 rows.

Real-life case: This is the exact mechanism behind an unexpected "fan-out" — joining a fact table to a dimension that isn't actually unique on the key silently multiplies row counts and inflates sums.

Say: Rows with NULL in the join column won't match anything in a standard INNER or OUTER JOIN, since NULL is never considered equal to another NULL in a join comparison — those rows simply get excluded (or appear with NULLs on the other side in an OUTER JOIN).

Real-life case: I've seen this surface as "missing" rows in a report that turned out to be legitimate records with a blank foreign key — the fix was deciding whether those really belonged in the join at all, or needed a default/unknown-member row in the dimension.

Say: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table regardless of a match, so filtering on NULL from the right table's key isolates exactly the unmatched rows.

Query:

SELECT e.*
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN Salary s ON e.EmpID = s.EmpID
WHERE s.EmpID IS NULL;

Real-life case: I use this exact LEFT JOIN + IS NULL pattern whenever I need to find orphan or unmatched records between a master and a transaction table — for example, records present in one feed but missing from another on a data-quality check.

Related Questions

Because this is the generic version of the exact same LEFT JOIN + IS NULL orphan-record pattern.

Say:

"I'll use a LEFT JOIN and find records where Table B has no match."

SELECT a.*
FROM TableA a
LEFT JOIN TableB b
    ON a.ID = b.ID
WHERE b.ID IS NULL;

Normally, NULL values do not match other NULL values using a standard equality condition — for example ON A.ID = B.ID. If both IDs are NULL, the comparison is not TRUE, so those rows do not match in an INNER JOIN.

An INNER JOIN only returns rows where the join condition evaluates to TRUE.

It depends on the join type. INNER JOIN: rows with NULL join keys normally don't match. LEFT JOIN: all rows from the left table are retained; unmatched right-side columns become NULL. RIGHT JOIN: the opposite applies. FULL OUTER JOIN: unmatched rows from both tables are retained, with NULLs on the missing side.

Also, NULLs in non-key columns do not prevent a row from joining — the important factor is whether the join condition can be matched.

I would first identify the join key and count duplicates. If one value appears 2 times in Table A and 3 times in Table B, an INNER JOIN on that value will produce 2 × 3 = 6 rows, because every matching row in A combines with every matching row in B. Rows where the join key is NULL generally do not match under a normal A.Key = B.Key condition.

So when answering this type of question, I always check duplicate counts on both sides, matching key values, NULL behavior, and the resulting multiplication of duplicate matches.

SELECT
    a.AccountID,
    COUNT(t.TransactionID) AS MatchingTransactions
FROM Account a
LEFT JOIN Transactions t
    ON a.AccountID = t.AccountID
GROUP BY a.AccountID;

I'd use a LEFT JOIN if the requirement is to show all accounts, including accounts with zero transactions. If the requirement is only accounts that have matching transactions, an INNER JOIN is sufficient.

To validate the join, I'd compare total Account rows, distinct AccountIDs before and after the join, unmatched accounts, duplicate AccountIDs in the master table, and whether the transaction table causes the expected one-to-many row expansion.

Say: A CTE is a temporary named result set that exists for the duration of one SQL statement and makes complex logic easier to organize.

Query:

WITH SalesSummary AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(OrderValue) AS TotalSales
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT *
FROM SalesSummary;

Real-life case: Build customer sales first, rank them in the next step, and filter the final result.

Say: A CTE improves readability, breaks complex logic into steps, supports window functions and recursive queries, and is easier to maintain.

Real-life case: Separate aggregation, ranking and filtering instead of writing one large nested query.

Related Questions

Because this shows the readability advantage in action — breaking complex logic into a clean, named step.

Say:

"I'll use a CTE to break the complex logic into readable steps."

WITH SalesSummary AS (
    SELECT CustomerID,
           SUM(Amount) AS TotalSales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT CustomerID, TotalSales
FROM SalesSummary
WHERE TotalSales > 10000;

Say: A subquery is a query inside another query that provides an intermediate result to the outer query.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM Employees
WHERE Salary > (
    SELECT AVG(Salary)
    FROM Employees
);

Real-life case: Find employees whose salary is above the company average.

Say: I use a subquery for simple nested logic and a CTE when the query has multiple logical steps and needs better readability; neither is inherently faster.

Real-life case: Use a CTE for multi-step sales ranking and a subquery for a simple average comparison.

Say: A CTE is query-scoped, while a temporary table can store intermediate data, be indexed and reused across multiple statements.

Real-life case: Use a CTE for one reporting query; use a temp table when a large intermediate result is reused several times.

Say: Neither is universally faster; I would compare the execution plans and optimize based on the query, data volume and indexes.

Real-life case: If two equivalent queries perform differently, I would inspect the execution plan rather than assume the CTE is faster.

Say: A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so its result depends on the current outer row.

Query:

SELECT e.EmployeeName, e.Salary, e.DepartmentID
FROM Employees e
WHERE e.Salary > (
    SELECT AVG(e2.Salary)
    FROM Employees e2
    WHERE e2.DepartmentID = e.DepartmentID
);

Real-life case: Find employees earning above the average salary of their own department.

Yes. A CTE can be used with SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, as long as it is immediately followed by the statement that uses it.

For example, I can use a CTE to identify duplicate records and then delete the rows where the row number is greater than one. A CTE is basically a named temporary result set for a single statement.

Say: WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation, while HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

Query:

SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(order_value) AS total_sales
FROM Orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(order_value) > 100000;

Real-life case: First filter transactions to the required period, then keep only customers whose total sales exceed the threshold.

Say: Not directly in the normal query flow because WHERE filters rows before aggregation; use HAVING for aggregate conditions.

Incorrect:

WHERE SUM(order_value) > 100000

Correct:

HAVING SUM(order_value) > 100000

Real-life case: Filter high-value customers after calculating their total sales.

Related Questions

Because this is a real HAVING-based aggregate filter — the exact scenario where WHERE would fail and HAVING is required.

Say:

"Because I'm filtering an aggregate, I'll use HAVING instead of WHERE."

SELECT DepartmentID,
       SUM(Salary) AS TotalSalary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY DepartmentID
HAVING SUM(Salary) > 100000;

Say: The logical order is FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → OFFSET-FETCH; TOP is part of the SELECT operation in SQL Server.

Real-life case: Understanding the order explains why a WHERE filter happens before a grouped sales calculation.

Say: Whenever I need an aggregated result per category — total spend per region, count of orders per customer, average sales per product — GROUP BY collapses detail rows into one summary row per group so aggregate functions like SUM/COUNT/AVG can be applied.

Real-life case: Most of the summary views feeding the SAR dashboard use GROUP BY to roll transaction-level spend up to Region/Department/Month before Power BI ever sees the data.

Say: I would filter the salary records for 2023 using the WHERE clause, group the records by employee, and use SUM(salary) to calculate each employee's annual salary. Then I would use the HAVING clause to filter employees whose total salary is greater than ₹1 crore, which is ₹10,000,000.

SELECT
    employee_id,
    employee_name,
    SUM(salary) AS annual_salary
FROM employee_salary
WHERE salary_date >= '2023-01-01'
  AND salary_date < '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY
    employee_id,
    employee_name
HAVING SUM(salary) > 10000000;

Key point: WHERE filters rows before grouping, while HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

Yes. If GROUP BY is not specified, the entire result set can be treated as a single group.

SELECT SUM(SalesAmount) AS TotalSales
FROM Sales
HAVING SUM(SalesAmount) > 100000;

However, in most practical cases, HAVING is commonly used together with GROUP BY to filter aggregated groups.

Say: I use ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by customer and ordered by date descending, then keep rn = 1.

Query:

WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id
               ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Orders
)
SELECT *
FROM Ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

Real-life case: Get each customer's latest purchase.

Related Questions

Because this uses the exact same ROW_NUMBER() + PARTITION BY pattern, just filtering for rn = 2 instead of rn = 1.

Say:

"I'll use ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by customer and order by date descending."

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY CustomerID
               ORDER BY OrderDate DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Orders
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rn = 2;

Say: I aggregate sales by category and product, rank products within each category, and keep rank 1; with DENSE_RANK() I include ties.

Query:

WITH ProductSales AS (
    SELECT category,
           product_id,
           SUM(sales) AS total_sales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY category, product_id
),
Ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY category
               ORDER BY total_sales DESC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM ProductSales
)
SELECT category, product_id, total_sales
FROM Ranked
WHERE rnk = 1;

Real-life case: Identify the best-selling SKU in every product category.

Related Questions

Because this is the direct hands-on version of the same aggregate-then-rank-within-category pattern.

Say:

"I'll rank products within each category and select rank one."

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT ProductID, Category,
           SUM(SalesAmount) AS TotalSales,
           RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY Category
               ORDER BY SUM(SalesAmount) DESC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY ProductID, Category
)
SELECT *
FROM CTE
WHERE rnk = 1;

Say: I aggregate product sales, use DENSE_RANK() with PARTITION BY category, and filter for rank \\<= N when I want to include ties; for exactly N products per category, I use ROW_NUMBER().

Query:

WITH ProductSales AS (
    SELECT category,
           product_id,
           SUM(sales) AS total_sales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY category, product_id
),
Ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY category
               ORDER BY total_sales DESC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM ProductSales
)
SELECT *
FROM Ranked
WHERE rnk <= 3;

Exactly 3 products per category:

WITH ProductSales AS (
    SELECT category,
           product_id,
           SUM(sales) AS total_sales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY category, product_id
),
Ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY category
               ORDER BY total_sales DESC, product_id
           ) AS rn
    FROM ProductSales
)
SELECT *
FROM Ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;

Real-life case: Use this version when the requirement is exactly three products per category; use DENSE_RANK() when tied products should all be included.

Real-life case: Show the top three products in every category on a Power BI report.

Say: I group by customer, calculate total sales, and use HAVING to filter the aggregated result.

Query:

SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(order_value) AS total_sales
FROM Orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(order_value) > 100000;

Real-life case: Identify high-value customers for management reporting.

Related Questions

Because this is the same GROUP BY + HAVING threshold pattern applied to departments instead of customers.

Say:

"Because I'm filtering an aggregate, I'll use HAVING instead of WHERE."

SELECT DepartmentID,
       SUM(Salary) AS TotalSalary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY DepartmentID
HAVING SUM(Salary) > 100000;

Say: A simple filtered query combining a value threshold with a date/year condition on whichever column represents the relevant year.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM Employee
WHERE Salary > 10000000
  AND YEAR(JoiningOrSalaryDate) = 2023;

Real-life case: I'd confirm with the interviewer which date column represents "in 2023" — salary effective date, joining date, or review date — since that changes the actual filter column even though the query shape stays the same.

The usual culprit is a filter condition on the right-table column sitting in the WHERE clause instead of the ON clause — that silently converts the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN because rows where the right side is NULL get filtered out. Other causes: a case-sensitivity or trailing-space mismatch on the join key, or the right table actually being aggregated/deduplicated earlier in the query in a way that drops rows. First thing I check is always where the filter on the right table sits.

I’d pull the execution plan first to see if the new join introduced a table scan instead of an index seek — usually means there’s no index on the join key. Other checks: whether I’m pulling more columns than needed (SELECT *), whether filtering happens early enough to reduce rows before the join, join order, and whether an EXISTS would be cheaper than the join if I only need to check for a match rather than pull columns from the second table.

Say: UNION combines result sets and removes duplicate rows, while UNION ALL combines them without removing duplicates and generally has less overhead.

Query:

SELECT customer_id FROM Customers_2025
UNION
SELECT customer_id FROM Customers_2026;

SELECT customer_id FROM Customers_2025
UNION ALL
SELECT customer_id FROM Customers_2026;

Real-life case: Use UNION for a distinct customer list and UNION ALL when every transaction row must be preserved.

Say: UNION ALL generally performs better because it does not need duplicate elimination.

Real-life case: Combine monthly transaction tables with UNION ALL when duplicate removal is not required.

Say: LIKE performs pattern matching on string values.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM Customers
WHERE customer_name LIKE 'A%';

Real-life case: Find customers whose names begin with a specific character.

Say: % matches zero or more characters, while _ matches exactly one character.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM Customers
WHERE name LIKE 'A%';   -- starts with A

SELECT *
FROM Customers
WHERE name LIKE '%A';   -- ends with A

SELECT *
FROM Customers
WHERE name LIKE '%an%'; -- contains an

SELECT *
FROM Customers
WHERE name LIKE 'A_';   -- A + exactly one character

Real-life case: Search customer/product names using flexible text patterns.

Say: ISNULL replaces a NULL, COALESCE returns the first non-NULL expression, and NULLIF returns NULL when two expressions are equal.

Query:

SELECT ISNULL(SalesAmount, 0)
FROM Sales;

SELECT COALESCE(HomePhone, WorkPhone, 'No Phone')
FROM Customers;

SELECT Sales / NULLIF(Quantity, 0)
FROM Sales;

Real-life case: Replace missing sales with zero, select a fallback phone number, or prevent divide-by-zero in KPI calculations.

Say: CASE implements conditional business logic similar to an IF-ELSE.

Query:

SELECT ProductName,
       Sales,
       CASE
           WHEN Sales >= 100000 THEN 'High'
           WHEN Sales >= 50000 THEN 'Medium'
           ELSE 'Low'
       END AS SalesCategory
FROM Products;

Real-life case: Classify inventory risk or sales performance into business-friendly categories; the source gives WOC examples of <5, 5–12, and >12.

Related Questions

Because this is the direct hands-on version of using CASE to build conditional categories.

Say:

"I'll use CASE WHEN to create conditional categories."

SELECT EmployeeID,
       Salary,
       CASE
           WHEN Salary < 50000 THEN 'Low'
           WHEN Salary < 100000 THEN 'Medium'
           ELSE 'High'
       END AS SalaryCategory
FROM Employees;

Because this shows a second, more advanced CASE pattern — conditional aggregation for pivoting rows into columns.

Say:

"I'll use conditional aggregation with CASE WHEN."

SELECT CustomerID,
       SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Jan' THEN Sales ELSE 0 END) AS JanSales,
       SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Feb' THEN Sales ELSE 0 END) AS FebSales,
       SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Mar' THEN Sales ELSE 0 END) AS MarSales
FROM Sales
GROUP BY CustomerID;

Say: It returns zero rows — in SQL, NULL represents an unknown value, so NULL = NULL evaluates to unknown (not true), and the WHERE clause only keeps rows where the condition evaluates to true.

Real-life case: This is exactly why you use IS NULL instead of = NULL to actually find NULL rows — a classic gotcha that trips people up in interviews and in real queries alike.

Say: I haven't used BLOB-style storage in my project work. In SQL Server, the equivalent for storing binary/large object data is VARBINARY(MAX); my project data was structured relational data, not binary files.

Real-life case: If a future project needed to store scanned documents or images alongside transactional data, VARBINARY(MAX) would be the SQL Server type to reach for.

Say: NVARCHAR, since it stores Unicode data and supports multilingual characters, unlike VARCHAR which is limited to a single character set. NVARCHAR(MAX) can store up to roughly 2GB of character data; a fixed-length NVARCHAR(n) supports up to 4,000 characters.

Real-life case: Any customer- or vendor-name field that might contain non-English characters should be NVARCHAR from the start — retrofitting it after data has already been mangled by VARCHAR is much harder.

Say: A Primary Key uniquely identifies each row in a table and cannot contain duplicate or NULL values.

Query:

CREATE TABLE Customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name VARCHAR(100)
);

Real-life case: CustomerID uniquely identifies each customer.

Say: A Foreign Key creates a relationship by referencing a Primary Key or unique key in another table.

Query:

CREATE TABLE Orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES Customers(customer_id)
);

Real-life case: Orders.CustomerID connects each order to the customer table.
