Say: The Primary Key identifies a row in its own table, while the Foreign Key connects a row to another table.

Real-life case: CustomerID is the PK in Customers and the FK in Orders.

Say: A Candidate Key is a column or combination of columns that can uniquely identify a row and is eligible to become the Primary Key.

Real-life case: If both EmployeeID and Email are unique, both can be candidate keys.

Say: An Alternate Key is a candidate key that was not selected as the Primary Key.

Real-life case: EmployeeID is the PK while a unique email can be an alternate key.

Say: A Composite Key uses two or more columns together to uniquely identify a row.

Query:

CREATE TABLE OrderDetails (
    order_id INT,
    product_id INT,
    quantity INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

Real-life case: In an order-detail table, OrderID + ProductID can uniquely identify a product line.

Say: A Surrogate Key is a system-generated, meaningless unique identifier commonly used in data warehouses and dimension tables.

Real-life case: Use product_sk as the primary key of a Product dimension while retaining the business product_id.

Say: If it uniquely identifies its own row use PK; if it references another table use FK; if it only needs uniqueness use a Unique Key.

Real-life case: CustomerID = PK in Customers, CustomerID = FK in Orders, Email = UNIQUE.

Say: Primary Key: no NULLs, no duplicates, one per table, creates a clustered index by default. Unique Key: no duplicates but allows one NULL, non-clustered index by default. Foreign Key: enforces referential integrity to a parent table's key, and itself allows duplicates and NULLs.

Real-life case: On the SAR model I used a surrogate key as the PK on each dimension table (clustered), a Unique Key on the natural business code where one existed (to catch accidental duplicates without blocking a legitimate blank), and FKs on the fact table linking back to each dimension.

Numeric surrogate keys are generally preferred because they're smaller, more consistent, and more efficient for relationships than long text values. Text keys can suffer from spelling differences, case or formatting inconsistencies, changes in business names, and larger storage requirements.

For example, instead of relating tables using "North America Finance Department", I'd prefer an integer key such as DepartmentKey.

Say: A clustered index organizes table data around the index key and a table can have one, while a non-clustered index is a separate structure and multiple can exist.

Real-life case: Use an appropriate clustered index for common range/sequential access and non-clustered indexes for frequently searched columns.

Say: Indexing means storing table data in a sorted/organized way so that data retrieval (read operations) becomes faster. An index is a database object that speeds up data retrieval by creating a lookup structure on one or more columns. Indexing is the process of creating and using these indexes to improve query performance and reduce full table scans.

Real-life case: Think of it like the index section of a book that helps you find a topic quickly — instead of reading every page (a full table scan), you jump straight to the right one.

Say: An execution plan shows how SQL Server will actually run a query — the scans, seeks, joins, sorting, and estimated costs — and it's the main tool for diagnosing why a query is slow.

Real-life case: I've taken a 30-second query down to about 2 seconds by reading the plan and fixing what it flagged — table scans on large tables, missing indexes, expensive sort operators, and large hash matches were the usual culprits.

Say: DELETE removes selected rows and supports WHERE; TRUNCATE removes all rows while keeping the table; DROP removes the table object.

Query:

DELETE FROM Employees
WHERE Department = 'HR';

TRUNCATE TABLE Employees;

DROP TABLE Employees;

Real-life case: Delete selected bad records with DELETE; clear a staging table with TRUNCATE; remove an obsolete table with DROP.

Say: For removing all rows, TRUNCATE is generally more efficient than row-by-row DELETE; DROP removes the table object entirely, and actual performance depends on the operation and execution plan.

Real-life case: For clearing a staging table completely, TRUNCATE is generally preferable to row-by-row DELETE.

Say: I'd use CONVERT() or TRY_CONVERT() with the right style code, e.g. CONVERT(date, '2026-08-19', 23), or TRY_CAST() if the format is safe to assume — the TRY_ variants avoid errors on bad data by returning NULL instead of failing the whole query.

Real-life case: Raw source extracts often store dates as strings — I use TRY_CONVERT(date, col, 23) in the staging query so bad rows become NULL instead of failing the entire load.

Say: PIVOT turns row values into columns — for example monthly sales as separate columns — while UNPIVOT does the reverse, turning columns back into rows for normalized reporting.

Query:

SELECT *
FROM (SELECT Month, Amount FROM Sales) src
PIVOT (
    SUM(Amount) FOR Month IN ([Jan], [Feb], [Mar])
) AS pvt;

Real-life case: Used PIVOT to convert month-wise columns into a single Month/Value pair, the exact shape a Power BI star schema needs for time intelligence.

Say: I'd use CHARINDEX() to find the position of "@" and SUBSTRING() to extract everything after it.

Query:

SELECT SUBSTRING(Email, CHARINDEX('@', Email) + 1, LEN(Email))
FROM Contacts;

Real-life case: Used this exact pattern while cleaning a large recruiter/contact list to extract and validate company domains for segmentation.

Say: I'd join current-year and prior-year aggregates (or use LAG() over a yearly partition) and calculate (CurrentYear - PriorYear) / PriorYear.

Query:

WITH Yearly AS (
    SELECT YEAR(SaleDate) AS Yr, SUM(Amount) AS Revenue
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY YEAR(SaleDate)
)
SELECT Yr, Revenue,
       LAG(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY Yr) AS PriorYearRevenue,
       (Revenue - LAG(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY Yr)) * 1.0
           / NULLIF(LAG(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY Yr), 0) AS YoYGrowth
FROM Yearly;

Real-life case: Built a YoY revenue growth measure in DAX for the SAR dashboard, and validated the numbers first with a SQL query like this against the raw source.

Say: I'd join customers active in Month N with customers active in Month N-1 on CustomerID — an INNER JOIN gives retained customers; a LEFT JOIN with a NULL check (or EXCEPT) gives churned customers.

Query:

SELECT DISTINCT curr.CustomerID
FROM MonthlyActive curr
JOIN MonthlyActive prev
    ON curr.CustomerID = prev.CustomerID
    AND curr.MonthNum = prev.MonthNum + 1;

Real-life case: Adapted this exact retention logic to track which stores remained active recipients month-over-month for a supply consistency check on the SAR project.

Related Questions

Because this solves the same consecutive-month retention problem with a different technique — LAG() instead of a self-join on offset month numbers.

Say:

"I'll compare each purchase month with the previous purchase month using LAG()."

Say: IN compares a value with a list/result set, while EXISTS checks whether at least one related row exists; NOT IN needs special care with NULLs.

Query:

\-- IN
SELECT *
FROM Customers
WHERE CustomerID IN (
    SELECT CustomerID
    FROM Orders
);

\-- EXISTS
SELECT *
FROM Customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM Orders o
    WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
);

Real-life case: Use EXISTS when checking whether a customer has any order.

Say: I start with all customers and use NOT EXISTS to return customers with no order in the last six months.

Query:

SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
FROM Customer c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM Orders o
    WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
      AND o.OrderDate >= DATEADD(MONTH, -6, GETDATE())
);

Real-life case: Identify inactive customers for a retention or re-engagement campaign.

Related Questions

Because this is the exact same problem solved with an alternate technique — GROUP BY + HAVING MAX() instead of NOT EXISTS.

Say:

"I'll find customers whose latest purchase is older than six months or who have never purchased."

SELECT CustomerID
FROM Orders
GROUP BY CustomerID
HAVING MAX(OrderDate) < DATEADD(MONTH, -6, GETDATE());

Say: FIRST_VALUE() returns the first value in a window per the PARTITION BY and ORDER BY clauses, which is useful for finding an initial event per group.

Query:

SELECT
    CustomerID,
    OrderDate,
    FIRST_VALUE(OrderDate) OVER (
        PARTITION BY CustomerID
        ORDER BY OrderDate
    ) AS FirstPurchase
FROM Orders;

Real-life case: I'd use this to find each customer's very first purchase date for a customer-journey or cohort analysis.

Related Questions

Because this solves the same problem with an alternate technique — MIN()/MAX() with GROUP BY instead of FIRST_VALUE()/LAST_VALUE() window functions.

Say:

"I'll use MIN() for the first purchase and MAX() for the last purchase."

SELECT CustomerID,
       MIN(PurchaseDate) AS FirstPurchase,
       MAX(PurchaseDate) AS LastPurchase
FROM Orders
GROUP BY CustomerID;

Say: LAST_VALUE() returns the last value in the window, but without an explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame it only looks at rows up to the current row, which usually gives the wrong answer.

Query:

SELECT
    CustomerID,
    OrderDate,
    LAST_VALUE(OrderDate) OVER (
        PARTITION BY CustomerID
        ORDER BY OrderDate
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
        AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
    ) AS LastPurchase
FROM Orders;

Real-life case: I always add the explicit frame when using LAST_VALUE() to find each customer's most recent purchase — leaving it out is one of the most common SQL interview traps.

Related Questions

Because this solves the same last-value problem with the simpler MIN()/MAX() technique — no frame-clause pitfall to worry about.

Say:

"I'll filter the required date range and then use MIN() and MAX()."

SELECT CustomerID,
       MIN(TransactionDate) AS FirstTransaction,
       MAX(TransactionDate) AS LastTransaction
FROM Transactions
WHERE TransactionDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-06-30'
GROUP BY CustomerID;

Say: A transaction groups one or more database operations into one logical unit that can be committed or rolled back.

Query:

BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;

    UPDATE Accounts
    SET Balance = Balance - 500
    WHERE AccountID = 1;

    UPDATE Accounts
    SET Balance = Balance + 500
    WHERE AccountID = 2;

    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0
        ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;

    THROW;
END CATCH;

Real-life case: A transfer should debit one account and credit another as one logical unit; if either operation fails, the transaction is rolled back.

Say: ACID means Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability: all-or-nothing, valid state, controlled concurrency, and persistence after commit.

Real-life case: A financial transaction must either complete fully or roll back without leaving inconsistent balances.

Say: Normalization organizes data into related tables to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity.

Real-life case: Instead of repeating customer information on every order row, store customer details once and reference them through CustomerID.

Say: It reduces redundancy, improves consistency and prevents insert, update and delete anomalies.

Real-life case: Updating a customer's city in one Customers table is safer than updating the same city repeatedly across thousands of order rows.

Say: 1NF removes repeating groups and requires atomic values; 2NF removes partial dependency on part of a composite key; 3NF removes transitive dependency between non-key attributes.

Real-life case: Split customer, order and product information into appropriate related tables instead of storing repeated attributes in one large table.

Say: Denormalization intentionally combines tables to reduce joins and speed up reads, trading some storage and redundancy for faster reporting.

Real-life case: Instead of joining Product and Category every time, I'd store CategoryName directly on the Product table for a reporting layer — faster queries, at the cost of extra storage and the risk of redundant data going out of sync.

30-second answer: "My main SQL optimization techniques are selecting only required columns, filtering early, using appropriate indexes, avoiding unnecessary joins and subqueries, checking execution plans, optimizing joins and aggregations, avoiding functions on indexed columns where possible, and ensuring statistics are updated. I also look for unnecessary scans and high-cost operators."

Techniques to remember:

-- 1. Indexing
CREATE INDEX IX_Sales_Product
ON Sales(ProductID);

-- 2. Avoid SELECT *
-- Prefer:
SELECT ProductID, Sales
FROM Sales;

3. Filter early    4. Optimize JOINs    5. Check the execution plan    6. Avoid unnecessary DISTINCT    7. Avoid functions on indexed columns    8. Update statistics when appropriate.

Real-life case: "If a sales query takes 30 seconds, I check the execution plan. If I see a table scan on a large transaction table, I investigate whether an appropriate index can reduce the scan."

30-second answer: "First, I reproduce the problem and check the execution plan to identify the expensive operation. I look for table scans, expensive joins, missing indexes, large sorts, excessive aggregations and inaccurate cardinality estimates. Then I optimize the query by filtering early, selecting only required columns, simplifying joins or subqueries and adding or modifying indexes when appropriate. Finally, I compare execution time and the execution plan before and after the change."

Interview flow:

Slow Query
   ↓
Execution Plan
   ↓
Find Bottleneck
   ↓
Scan? / Join? / Sort? / Aggregation? / Missing Index?
   ↓
Optimize
   ↓
Test Again
   ↓
Compare Performance

Real-life case: "A sales query joining a 100-million-row transaction table with several dimensions takes 40 seconds. The execution plan shows a large table scan. I would check filtering, indexes and join conditions, then test the revised query against the original execution plan."

Yes. My approach is to first identify where the bottleneck is rather than immediately rewriting the query — I check the execution plan, table size, joins, filters, indexes, unnecessary columns, and whether functions are being applied to indexed columns.

Some techniques I use: filtering data as early as possible, avoiding SELECT *, checking indexes on join and filter columns, removing unnecessary joins, avoiding functions on filter columns where possible, using appropriate joins and aggregating at the required grain, replacing repeated logic with reusable views, and checking for duplicate-driven join explosions.

In my reporting work, I also try to push heavy transformations into SQL views rather than doing everything in Power Query or DAX.

Say: A View is a stored SQL query that presents its result as a virtual table; a normal View does not physically store the result set.

Query:

CREATE VIEW vw_customer_sales AS
SELECT CustomerID,
       SUM(OrderValue) AS TotalSales
FROM Orders
GROUP BY CustomerID;

Real-life case: The source specifically describes SQL Views such as vw_kpi_master being used to standardize KPI logic for Power BI dashboards.

Say: A normal View does not accept parameters, complex views can become difficult to maintain, and complex underlying queries can affect performance.

Real-life case: If a Power BI report needs parameterized database logic, consider a stored procedure, parameterized query or table-valued function rather than a normal View.

Say: No; a standard SQL Server View cannot declare local variables.

*Example of invalid View logic:*

DECLARE @StartDate DATE;

Real-life case: Use another database object or parameterized approach when the reporting logic needs runtime parameters.

Say: A SQL variable is temporary named storage used during execution of a batch, procedure or script.

Query:

DECLARE @TotalSales DECIMAL(18,2);
SET @TotalSales = 100000;
SELECT @TotalSales;

Real-life case: Store an intermediate threshold or calculation while running a SQL script.

Say: In DAX, VAR stores an expression result so it can be reused and makes a measure easier to read.

Query:

Sales Growth % =
VAR CurrentSales = [Total Sales]
VAR PreviousSales = [Previous Year Sales]
RETURN
    DIVIDE(CurrentSales - PreviousSales, PreviousSales)

Real-life case: Reuse current and previous sales values inside a Power BI measure.

Say: A Stored Procedure performs database operations, while a Function returns a reusable value or table.

Real-life case: A procedure can handle a multi-step database operation; a function is suited to reusable calculation logic.

Say: "My primary SQL work was queries, analysis and SQL Views for Power BI reporting; Stored Procedures were not my primary development responsibility."

Real-life case: The source specifically positions the project work around SQL Views such as vw_kpi_master, so avoid claiming stored-procedure development as a primary responsibility.

Say: "I have used aggregate and window functions extensively, but creating user-defined SQL Functions was not a primary responsibility; my focus was SQL queries, Views and Power BI reporting."

Real-life case: Mention SUM, AVG, COUNT, ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG and LEAD as functions used in analysis.

Say: A Trigger is database logic that automatically fires when an event such as INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE occurs.

Query:

CREATE TRIGGER trg_Employee_Update
ON Employees
AFTER UPDATE
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO Employee_Audit
    (
        EmployeeID,
        EmployeeName,
        UpdatedDate
    )
    SELECT
        EmployeeID,
        EmployeeName,
        GETDATE()
    FROM inserted;
END;

Real-life case: Automatically create an audit record whenever an employee record is updated.

Say: A View is a saved SELECT query that behaves like a virtual table with no parameters, while a Stored Procedure is a precompiled program that can take parameters and contain logic, loops, and conditions.

Query:

CREATE VIEW vwSales AS
SELECT * FROM Sales;

CREATE PROCEDURE GetSales
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT * FROM Sales;
END

Real-life case: Power BI reads from a View for reporting, while nightly ETL jobs run through Stored Procedures for the actual data processing logic.

Say: A User-Defined Function is a reusable piece of SQL logic that returns either a scalar value or a table, which you can call inside other queries the same way you'd call a built-in function like SUM() or GETDATE().

Query:

CREATE FUNCTION dbo.fn_GetFiscalYear (@OrderDate DATE)
RETURNS INT
AS
BEGIN
    RETURN YEAR(DATEADD(MONTH, 3, @OrderDate))
END

Real-life case: A scalar function like this could standardize fiscal-year logic across multiple queries instead of repeating the same CASE/DATEADD expression everywhere.

Say: SQL Server doesn't have a Materialized View in the Oracle/PostgreSQL sense — the closest equivalent is an Indexed View, which physically stores the result set and updates it as underlying data changes.

Real-life case: You'd reach for an Indexed View when a query is run very frequently and the underlying joins/aggregations are expensive, and a regular View's on-the-fly execution is too slow — I haven't used Indexed Views directly in my project, since my views like vw_kpi_master were kept as standard views.

Say: My optimization work has mainly been at the query and view level — adding appropriate WHERE filters earlier, avoiding unnecessary SELECT *, and restructuring joins so indexed columns are used for the join key, rather than a single dramatic before/after story on a specific query.

Real-life case: General approach: check the execution plan, look for table scans that could become index seeks, and reduce the data volume before joining rather than after.

Say: My hands-on SQL work centered on queries and views rather than procedural error-handling logic in Stored Procedures. Conceptually, that's done with TRY...CATCH blocks, where the CATCH block can log the error details (using ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_NUMBER()) or roll back a transaction cleanly.

Query:

BEGIN TRY
    UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 100 WHERE AccountID = 1;
    UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + 100 WHERE AccountID = 2;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    INSERT INTO ErrorLog (Message, ErrorNumber, LoggedAt)
    VALUES (ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_NUMBER(), GETDATE());
END CATCH

Real-life case: I'd present this concept accurately in an interview without claiming hands-on ownership I don't have.

Say: I'd check the execution plan for expensive operations like table scans, look for missing indexes on join/filter columns, check for excessive use of cursors or row-by-row logic that could be set-based instead, and see if the procedure can be broken into smaller, testable steps to isolate the slow part.

Real-life case: With a procedure that large, I'd rather isolate and time each major section first than guess at an optimization — the slowest 10% of the logic is usually responsible for most of the runtime.

Say: A temporary table stores intermediate data temporarily and is useful when results must be reused or indexed across multiple steps.

Query:

CREATE TABLE #TempSales (
    CustomerID INT,
    TotalSales DECIMAL(18,2)
);

Real-life case: Store a large intermediate customer-sales result before joining it to another dataset.

Say: #Temp is local to the current session/scope, while ##Temp can be accessed by multiple sessions.

Query:

CREATE TABLE #Sales (...);
CREATE TABLE ##Sales (...);

Real-life case: Use a local temp table for your session-specific analysis; use a global one only when cross-session sharing is required.

Say: A Table Variable is scoped to the current batch, has limited statistics for the query optimizer, and generally suits small datasets; a Temp Table behaves more like a regular table, supports indexes, and the optimizer has better statistics for it, making it a better fit for larger intermediate datasets.

Real-life case: I'd reach for a table variable for a small lookup set inside a single batch, but switch to a temp table the moment the intermediate result gets large enough that indexing and accurate row-count estimates start to matter.

Say: A recursive CTE references itself and is used for hierarchical data such as employee-manager relationships.

Query:

WITH EmployeeHierarchy AS (
    SELECT EmployeeID, EmployeeName, ManagerID
    FROM Employees
    WHERE ManagerID IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    SELECT e.EmployeeID, e.EmployeeName, e.ManagerID
    FROM Employees e
    INNER JOIN EmployeeHierarchy h
        ON e.ManagerID = h.EmployeeID
)
SELECT *
FROM EmployeeHierarchy;

Real-life case: Build an organizational hierarchy from manager to employee.

Say: TOP returns a specified number of rows in SQL Server, while OFFSET-FETCH skips rows and returns the next requested rows.

Query:

SELECT TOP 3 *
FROM Employees
ORDER BY Salary DESC;

Real-life case: Return the top three products by sales or paginate a result set.

ConceptOne-line memory
ROW_NUMBER()Unique numbering
RANK()Ties + gaps
DENSE_RANK()Ties + no gaps
Window FunctionCalculate across rows without collapsing
PARTITION BYGroups for a window calculation
OVER()Defines the window
LAG()Previous row
LEAD()Next row
GROUP BYGroups + collapses
CTENamed temporary result for one statement
SubqueryQuery inside another query
Correlated SubqueryInner query depends on outer row
INNER JOINMatching rows
LEFT JOINAll left + matching right
RIGHT JOINAll right + matching left
FULL JOINEverything from both
CROSS JOINEvery combination
SELF JOINTable joined to itself
UNIONCombines + removes duplicates
UNION ALLCombines + keeps duplicates
LIKEPattern matching
WHEREFilters rows before aggregation
HAVINGFilters groups after aggregation
Primary KeyUniquely identifies row
Foreign KeyConnects tables
Candidate KeyCan become PK
Alternate KeyCandidate key not selected as PK
Composite KeyMultiple columns form key

ViewReusable virtual table

Stored ProcedurePerforms operations/business process

Non-Clustered IndexSeparate lookup structure
ISNULL()Replace NULL

*For theory:*\\ \\> "One-line definition + when I use it."

*For SQL coding:*\\ \\> "First I identify the required grain, then filter/aggregate, apply the appropriate join or window function, and finally filter/order the result."

*For real-life scenarios:*\\ \\> "I would first clarify the business requirement, identify the correct tables and keys, validate duplicates/nulls, write the query, and verify the result before using it in reporting."

HR SCREENING QUESTIONS

Common HR / screening-round questions with ready-to-say answers, grounded in real project metrics.

Hi, I'm Nayan Bobde. I have around 2.5 years of experience as a Data Analyst, primarily working in Retail and Supply Chain Analytics at Cognizant.

My core skills are SQL and Power BI, along with DAX, Power Query, Data Modeling, Advanced Excel, Python, and Microsoft Fabric. I completed PL-300 Power BI Data Analyst and DP-600 Microsoft Fabric Analytics Engineer certifications, which strengthened my analytics and reporting capabilities.

My analytics journey started with SQL-based data extraction and reporting. Over time, I moved into end-to-end analytics, including requirement gathering, data validation, KPI development, dashboard design, stakeholder management, and business insights generation.

I worked with a global apparel retail client where I analyzed inventory movement from Distribution Centers to stores, allocation performance, stock availability, and inventory optimization. I worked with over 500K records and 20,000+ SKUs and developed Power BI dashboards for Buying, Planning, Merchandising, Supply Chain, and Distribution teams.

My most recent project was the Global Direct SAR Dashboard, where I developed financial and spend analytics reports using SQL and Power BI, handling custom fiscal-year calculations, multi-currency conversion, and dynamic security.

Overall, my role has been to convert raw business data into meaningful insights that help stakeholders make better business decisions.

The primary reason is that my project ended, and there were limited internal opportunities aligned with my skills and career goals.

After spending more than two years developing strong analytics skills in retail and supply chain analytics, I wanted my next role to provide deeper exposure to data analytics, reporting, cloud analytics, and stakeholder-facing work.

That's why I'm looking for an opportunity that aligns better with my long-term career path.

The project objective was to improve inventory visibility and allocation decisions across the retail supply chain.

The data came from SQL Server, JDA allocation systems, inventory systems, and sales data. I extracted and validated the data using SQL and performed transformations through SQL and Power Query.

The dashboard became a centralized source of truth for spend analysis across departments and regions, helping leadership make faster and more informed financial decisions.
